  1|# DevSecOps Pipeline Patterns
  2|
  3|Integrating security into every stage of the CI/CD pipeline, shifting detection left and enforcing automated gates.
  4|
  5|## Shift-Left Security Principles
  6|
  7|- Find vulnerabilities as early as possible: in the IDE, at commit time, and during CI — not after deployment.
  8|- Make security checks fast and non-blocking in early stages (warnings), then enforcing (gates) in later stages.
  9|- Treat security findings like bugs: track, prioritize, and fix them within normal sprint cycles.
 10|- Security is a shared responsibility, not a gatekeeping function. Enable developers with tooling and education.
 11|
 12|## SAST — Static Application Security Testing
 13|
 14|**Purpose**: Analyse source code for vulnerabilities without executing it.
 15|
 16|**Tools**:
 17|- **Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer**: ML-powered code review for Java and Python. Integrates with CodeCommit and GitHub.
 18|- **SonarQube / SonarCloud**: Multi-language static analysis. Covers security, reliability, maintainability.
 19|- **Semgrep**: Lightweight, pattern-based scanning. Fast, supports custom rules, good for enforcing team standards.
 20|- **Bandit** (Python), **ESLint security plugins** (JavaScript/TypeScript).
 21|
 22|**Pipeline Integration**:
 23|- Run SAST on every pull request. Report findings as PR comments or annotations.
 24|- Define severity thresholds: block merges on Critical/High findings; warn on Medium.
 25|- Maintain a suppression file for accepted risks (with justification and expiry date).
 26|
 27|## DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing
 28|
 29|**Purpose**: Test the running application by sending crafted requests to find runtime vulnerabilities.
 30|
 31|- Run against staging or ephemeral environments, not production.
 32|- Tools: OWASP ZAP (open source), Burp Suite (commercial), AWS Inspector for network scanning.
 33|- Integrate into the CD pipeline after deployment to a test environment.
 34|- DAST complements SAST; each catches different vulnerability classes.
 35|
 36|## Dependency Vulnerability Scanning
 37|
 38|**Purpose**: Detect known CVEs in third-party libraries and transitive dependencies.
 39|
 40|**Tools**:
 41|- **Amazon Inspector**: Scans EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and ECR images for software vulnerabilities.
 42|- **Snyk**: Developer-focused, supports npm, pip, Maven, Go modules. Provides fix PRs.
 43|- **Dependabot** (GitHub native): Automated dependency update PRs with vulnerability alerts.
 44|- **npm audit / pip-audit / cargo audit**: Built-in language-level tools for quick local checks.
 45|
 46|**Pipeline Integration**:
 47|- Scan on every build. Fail the build on Critical/High severity CVEs with known exploits.
 48|- Generate an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) using Syft or Trivy for supply chain transparency.
 49|- Review and update dependencies at least monthly; automate with Dependabot or Renovate.
 50|
 51|## IaC Security Scanning
 52|
 53|**Purpose**: Detect misconfigurations in infrastructure-as-code before deployment.
 54|
 55|**Tools**:
 56|- **cfn-lint**: CloudFormation linter. Validates syntax and best practices.
 57|- **cfn-nag**: CloudFormation static analysis. Finds overly permissive IAM policies, unencrypted resources.
 58|- **Checkov**: Multi-framework scanner (CloudFormation, Terraform, CDK, Kubernetes). Policy-as-code with custom rules.
 59|- **cdk-nag**: CDK-native. Checks CDK constructs against AWS Solutions rules and NIST/HIPAA packs.
 60|
 61|**Pipeline Integration**:
 62|- Run IaC scanning before `cdk synth` or `cfn deploy`. Fail the pipeline on High findings.
 63|- Use cdk-nag as a CDK Aspect so violations are caught at synthesis time, not after.
 64|- Maintain exception rules in code (not out-of-band) with mandatory justification comments.
 65|
 66|## Secret Detection
 67|
 68|**Purpose**: Prevent credentials, API keys, and tokens from being committed to source control.
 69|
 70|**Tools**:
 71|- **git-secrets** (AWS Labs): Pre-commit hook that blocks patterns matching AWS credentials.
 72|- **truffleHog**: Scans git history for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns.
 73|- **Gitleaks**: Fast, configurable, supports CI and pre-commit. Good default ruleset.
 74|- **GitHub secret scanning**: Built-in for GitHub repos; alerts on committed secrets from known providers.
 75|
 76|**Best Practices**:
 77|- Install pre-commit hooks for secret detection on every developer machine.
 78|- Run secret scanning in CI as a backup for missed pre-commit hooks.
 79|- If a secret is committed: revoke immediately, rotate, then clean git history.
 80|- Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, never in code or environment files.
 81|
 82|## Container Image Scanning
 83|
 84|**Purpose**: Detect OS-level and application-level vulnerabilities in container images.
 85|
 86|- **Amazon ECR image scanning**: Basic (Clair-based) and Enhanced (Inspector-powered) scanning.
 87|- **Trivy**: Comprehensive open-source scanner. Covers OS packages, language libraries, and IaC files.
 88|- Scan images on push to ECR and before deployment. Block deployment of images with Critical findings.
 89|- Use minimal base images (distroless, Alpine) to reduce attack surface.
 90|- Rebuild and rescan images weekly to pick up newly disclosed CVEs.
 91|
 92|## Security Gates in CI/CD
 93|
 94|Define clear pass/fail criteria at each pipeline stage:
 95|
 96|| Stage | Gate | Action on Failure |
 97||-------|------|-------------------|
 98|| Commit | Secret detection | Block commit (pre-commit hook) |
 99|| PR | SAST scan | Block merge on Critical/High |
100|| Build | Dependency scan | Fail build on Critical with exploit |
101|| Build | IaC scan | Fail build on High |
102|| Deploy to staging | DAST scan | Block promotion to production |
103|| Deploy to prod | Image scan | Block deployment on Critical |
104|| Post-deploy | Inspector continuous scan | Alert and create ticket |
105|
106|Automate exceptions with time-boxed waivers that require security team approval and auto-expire.
</file-view>

  1|# NFR Requirements Guide
  2|
  3|## Performance Requirement Benchmarking
  4|
  5|### How to Define Performance Requirements
  6|Every performance requirement must specify:
  7|- **Metric**: What is being measured (response time, throughput, resource usage)
  8|- **Target**: The quantitative threshold
  9|- **Percentile**: Which percentile the target applies to (p50, p95, p99)
 10|- **Load condition**: Under what concurrency/traffic the target must hold
 11|- **Measurement method**: How and where the metric is captured
 12|
 13|### Common Performance Targets by Application Type
 14|
 15|| Application Type | Metric | Target | Percentile | Notes |
 16||-----------------|--------|--------|------------|-------|
 17|| Web application (interactive) | Page load time | < 2s | p95 | First contentful paint |
 18|| REST API (synchronous) | Response time | < 200ms | p99 | Excludes network transit |
 19|| Search query | Result delivery | < 500ms | p95 | Including ranking |
 20|| Batch processing | Throughput | N records/min | Average | Define minimum acceptable rate |
 21|| Real-time messaging | End-to-end latency | < 100ms | p99 | From send to delivery |
 22|| File upload | Processing time | < 5s per MB | p95 | Post-upload processing |
 23|
 24|### Performance Anti-Requirements
 25|Explicitly exclude unreasonable expectations:
 26|- "The system should be fast" (not measurable)
 27|- "All pages load instantly" (no target, no percentile)
 28|- "Handle unlimited users" (no capacity boundary)
 29|
 30|Replace with: "The dashboard page loads in < 3 seconds at p95 under 500 concurrent users."
 31|
 32|## Scalability Assessment Frameworks
 33|
 34|### Capacity Planning Template
 35|
 36|| Dimension | Current | 6-Month Target | 12-Month Target | Scaling Mechanism |
 37||-----------|---------|---------------|-----------------|-------------------|
 38|| Concurrent users | N | N * X | N * Y | Horizontal auto-scaling |
 39|| Data volume | N GB | N * X GB | N * Y GB | Partitioning strategy |
 40|| Requests per second | N | N * X | N * Y | Load balancer + replicas |
 41|| Storage growth rate | N GB/month | N * X GB/month | N * Y GB/month | Tiered storage policy |
 42|
 43|### Scalability Requirement Format
 44|```
 45|NFR-SCALE-NNN: [Scalability Requirement]
 46|Current baseline: [measured current capacity]
 47|Target capacity: [required capacity at specific timeline]
 48|Growth model: [linear, exponential, seasonal, step-function]
 49|Scaling approach: [horizontal, vertical, partitioning, caching]
 50|Cost constraint: [infrastructure cost must remain below $X/month at target scale]
 51|Degradation policy: [what degrades first when approaching capacity limits]
 52|```
 53|
 54|### Scaling Decision Matrix
 55|
 56|| Signal | Scale Up | Scale Out | Optimize First |
 57||--------|----------|-----------|----------------|
 58|| CPU consistently > 70% | Single-instance workloads | Stateless services | Check for inefficient algorithms |
 59|| Memory pressure | In-memory processing | Distributed cache | Check for memory leaks |
 60|| I/O wait > 30% | Faster storage tier | Read replicas, sharding | Query optimization, indexing |
 61|| Queue depth growing | Faster consumers | More consumer instances | Batch size tuning |
 62|| Connection pool exhausted | Larger pool size | Connection multiplexing | Connection leak investigation |
 63|
 64|## Reliability Target-Setting
 65|
 66|### SLA/SLO/SLI Hierarchy
 67|
 68|| Term | Definition | Example | Who Defines |
 69||------|-----------|---------|-------------|
 70|| **SLI** (Indicator) | The metric being measured | Successful requests / total requests | Engineering |
 71|| **SLO** (Objective) | Internal target for the SLI | 99.95% success rate over 30 days | Engineering + Product |
 72|| **SLA** (Agreement) | External contractual commitment | 99.9% uptime with financial penalties | Business + Legal |
 73|
 74|**Rule**: SLO must be stricter than SLA. If SLA is 99.9%, set SLO at 99.95% to provide an internal buffer.
 75|
 76|### Availability Targets and Their Implications
 77|
 78|| Availability | Downtime / Year | Downtime / Month | Requires |
 79||-------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------|
 80|| 99% (two nines) | 3.65 days | 7.3 hours | Basic monitoring, manual recovery |
 81|| 99.9% (three nines) | 8.76 hours | 43.8 minutes | Auto-restart, health checks, alerting |
 82|| 99.95% | 4.38 hours | 21.9 minutes | Multi-AZ, automated failover, load balancing |
 83|| 99.99% (four nines) | 52.6 minutes | 4.38 minutes | Multi-region active-active, zero-downtime deploys |
 84|| 99.999% (five nines) | 5.26 minutes | 26.3 seconds | Fully automated everything, extensive redundancy |
 85|
 86|### Recovery Objectives
 87|
 88|| Objective | Definition | How to Set |
 89||-----------|-----------|------------|
 90|| **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective) | Maximum acceptable time to restore service | Based on business impact per hour of downtime |
 91|| **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective) | Maximum acceptable data loss window | Based on cost of recreating or losing data |
 92|| **MTTR** (Mean Time to Recovery) | Average time to restore from failure | Measured operationally; target should be < RTO |
 93|| **MTBF** (Mean Time Between Failures) | Average time between failures | Measured operationally; drives reliability investment |
 94|
 95|## Observability Requirements
 96|
 97|### Three Pillars Specification
 98|
 99|#### Metrics Requirements
100|Define for each component:
101|- **Business metrics**: Conversion rate, revenue processed, active users
102|- **Application metrics**: Request rate, error rate, latency (RED method)
103|- **Infrastructure metrics**: CPU, memory, disk, network (USE method)
104|- **Retention**: How long to keep each metric tier (1 min granularity for 7 days, 5 min for 30 days, 1 hour for 1 year)
105|
106|#### Logging Requirements
107|| Log Level | When to Use | Retention | Indexing |
108||-----------|------------|-----------|---------|
109|| ERROR | Unrecoverable failures requiring attention | 90 days | Full-text indexed |
110|| WARN | Recoverable issues, degraded behavior | 30 days | Full-text indexed |
111|| INFO | Significant business events, state transitions | 30 days | Structured fields only |
112|| DEBUG | Diagnostic detail for troubleshooting | 7 days | Not indexed (stored only) |
113|
114|#### Tracing Requirements
115|- Distributed traces across all service boundaries
116|- Trace context propagation via W3C Trace Context headers
117|- Sampling strategy: 100% for errors, 10% for normal traffic (adjust for volume)
118|- Trace retention: 7 days at full detail, 30 days for trace metadata
119|
120|### Alerting Requirements Template
121|For each alert:
122|```
123|Alert: [descriptive name]
124|SLI: [which service level indicator]
125|Threshold: [when to fire -- e.g., error rate > 1% for 5 minutes]
126|Severity: [page (wake someone up) | ticket (next business day) | log (informational)]
127|Runbook: [link to response procedure]
128|Notification: [who gets notified via which channel]
129|Auto-remediation: [if any automated response is triggered]
130|```
131|
132|### Observability Anti-Patterns to Avoid
133|- Alerting on causes instead of symptoms (alert on error rate, not CPU usage)
134|- Missing correlation IDs across service boundaries
135|- Logging sensitive data (PII, credentials, tokens)
136|- Alert fatigue from noisy thresholds (tune before deploying)
137|- Dashboard sprawl without clear ownership (every dashboard needs an owner)
138|
139|## Security Requirement Templates
140|
141|### Authentication Requirements
142|```
143|NFR-AUTH-NNN: [Authentication Requirement]
144|Method: [OAuth 2.0, JWT, session-based, API key, mTLS]
145|Token lifetime: [access token TTL, refresh token TTL]
146|MFA requirement: [none, optional, required for admin, required for all]
147|Session management: [max concurrent sessions, idle timeout, absolute timeout]
148|Password policy: [min length, complexity, rotation, breach detection]
149|```
150|
151|### Authorization Requirements
152|```
153|NFR-AUTHZ-NNN: [Authorization Requirement]
154|Model: [RBAC, ABAC, ACL, policy-based]
155|Roles: [list of roles and their permission boundaries]
156|Resource granularity: [organization, team, user, resource-level]
157|Delegation: [can users delegate permissions, under what constraints]
158|Audit: [which authorization decisions are logged]
159|```
160|
161|### Data Protection Requirements
162|```
163|NFR-DATA-NNN: [Data Protection Requirement]
164|Classification: [public, internal, confidential, restricted]
165|Encryption at rest: [algorithm, key management, rotation schedule]
166|Encryption in transit: [TLS version, cipher suites, certificate management]
167|PII handling: [identification, masking, pseudonymization, retention limits]
168|Data residency: [geographic constraints, cross-border transfer rules]
169|Backup encryption: [separate key, recovery testing frequency]
170|```
171|
172|### Compliance Requirements
173|```
174|NFR-COMP-NNN: [Compliance Requirement]
175|Framework: [GDPR, SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001]
176|Scope: [which components/data are in scope]
177|Controls: [specific controls required — access logging, encryption, retention]
178|Audit frequency: [continuous, quarterly, annual]
179|Evidence requirements: [what documentation/logs must be maintained]
180|```
181|
182|### Security Anti-Requirements
183|Explicitly exclude unreasonable expectations:
184|- "The system should be secure" (not measurable)
185|- "No vulnerabilities" (impossible — define acceptable risk)
186|- "Military-grade encryption" (undefined — specify algorithm and key length)
187|
188|Replace with: "All API endpoints require JWT authentication with RS256 signing. Access tokens expire after 15 minutes. Refresh tokens expire after 7 days and are single-use."

  1|# Security Guide
  2|
  3|## OWASP Top 10 (Application Security Checklist)
  4|
  5|For every application, verify defenses against each category:
  6|
  7|1. **Broken Access Control**: Enforce authorization on every endpoint. Deny by default. Verify object-level access (IDOR prevention). Disable directory listing. Invalidate sessions on logout.
  8|
  9|2. **Cryptographic Failures**: Use TLS 1.2+ for all data in transit. Encrypt sensitive data at rest (AES-256). Never store passwords in plaintext (use bcrypt/argon2 with salt). Do not roll custom crypto. Classify data sensitivity and protect accordingly.
 10|
 11|3. **Injection**: Parameterize all database queries (no string concatenation). Use ORM methods for queries. Validate and sanitize all input. Apply Content Security Policy headers. Encode output contextually (HTML, URL, JavaScript, CSS).
 12|
 13|4. **Insecure Design**: Threat model during design, not after. Limit resource consumption per user. Use secure design patterns (see below). Separate business logic from security controls.
 14|
 15|5. **Security Misconfiguration**: Remove default accounts and passwords. Disable unnecessary features and services. Set security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options). Keep dependencies patched. Review cloud service configurations (S3 bucket policies, security groups).
 16|
 17|6. **Vulnerable Components**: Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM). Scan dependencies weekly. Pin dependency versions. Have a process for emergency patching of critical CVEs. Remove unused dependencies.
 18|
 19|7. **Authentication Failures**: Implement rate limiting on login (5 attempts per minute). Enforce password complexity (12+ characters, no common passwords). Support MFA. Use secure session management (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies). Implement account lockout with notification.
 20|
 21|8. **Data Integrity Failures**: Verify integrity of software updates and CI/CD pipelines. Use signed artifacts. Validate data from untrusted sources. Protect deserialization (avoid accepting serialized objects from users).
 22|
 23|9. **Logging & Monitoring Failures**: Log authentication events (success and failure). Log access control failures. Log input validation failures. Do NOT log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII). Ship logs to centralized, tamper-resistant storage. Set up alerts for suspicious patterns.
 24|
 25|10. **SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)**: Validate and whitelist URLs for server-side requests. Block requests to internal networks (169.254.x.x, 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x). Disable HTTP redirects for server-initiated requests. Do not expose raw error messages from server-side requests.
 26|
 27|## STRIDE Threat Modeling
 28|
 29|For each component and data flow, assess:
 30|
 31|| Threat | Question | Example Mitigation |
 32||--------|----------|-------------------|
 33|| **S**poofing | Can an attacker impersonate a user or service? | Authentication, mutual TLS, API keys |
 34|| **T**ampering | Can data be modified in transit or at rest? | Input validation, checksums, signed tokens |
 35|| **R**epudiation | Can a user deny performing an action? | Audit logging, non-repudiation controls |
 36|| **I**nformation Disclosure | Can sensitive data leak? | Encryption, access controls, data masking |
 37|| **D**enial of Service | Can the system be made unavailable? | Rate limiting, autoscaling, circuit breakers |
 38|| **E**levation of Privilege | Can a user gain unauthorized permissions? | Least privilege, RBAC enforcement, input validation |
 39|
 40|## Authentication & Authorization Patterns
 41|
 42|### Authentication
 43|- **Session-based**: Server-side sessions with HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies. Best for server-rendered web apps.
 44|- **JWT**: Stateless tokens with short expiry (15 min access, 7 day refresh). Best for SPAs and APIs. Store access token in memory, refresh token in HttpOnly cookie.
 45|- **API Keys**: For service-to-service communication. Rotate regularly. Scope to minimum permissions.
 46|- **OAuth2/OIDC**: For third-party authentication delegation. Use authorization code flow with PKCE. Never use implicit flow.
 47|
 48|### Authorization
 49|- **RBAC (Role-Based)**: Assign permissions to roles, roles to users. Good for well-defined hierarchies.
 50|- **ABAC (Attribute-Based)**: Evaluate rules based on user, resource, action, and environment attributes. Good for complex, context-dependent policies.
 51|- **Object-Level**: Always verify the requesting user has access to the specific resource being requested. Never trust client-provided ownership claims.
 52|
 53|## Data Protection Requirements
 54|
 55|Classify data into tiers and apply controls:
 56|
 57|| Tier | Examples | At Rest | In Transit | Access | Retention |
 58||------|----------|---------|------------|--------|-----------|
 59|| Public | Marketing content | None required | HTTPS preferred | Open | Indefinite |
 60|| Internal | Business docs | Encrypted volume | HTTPS required | Authenticated | Per policy |
 61|| Confidential | PII, financial | AES-256, key rotation | TLS 1.2+ required | Role-restricted | Minimized |
 62|| Restricted | Passwords, keys | HSM/KMS, separate storage | mTLS | Named individuals | Shortest possible |
 63|
 64|## Secure Coding Practices Checklist
 65|
 66|For code review, verify:
 67|- [ ] All user input validated (type, length, range, format)
 68|- [ ] SQL queries parameterized (no string interpolation)
 69|- [ ] Output encoded for context (HTML, URL, JS)
 70|- [ ] Authentication checked on every protected endpoint
 71|- [ ] Authorization checked for the specific resource being accessed
 72|- [ ] Sensitive data not logged (passwords, tokens, PII)
 73|- [ ] Error messages do not reveal internal details (stack traces, SQL errors)
 74|- [ ] File uploads validated (type, size, scanned for malware)
 75|- [ ] CORS configured to allow only expected origins
 76|- [ ] Rate limiting applied to authentication and expensive operations
 77|- [ ] Secrets loaded from environment/secrets manager, never hardcoded

  1|# Threat Modelling with STRIDE
  2|
  3|A structured approach to identifying, classifying, and mitigating security threats during the design phase.
  4|
  5|## STRIDE Categories
  6|
  7|| Category | Threat | Violated Property | Example |
  8||----------|--------|-------------------|---------|
  9|| **S — Spoofing** | Attacker pretends to be another user or system | Authentication | Stolen JWT used to access another user's data |
 10|| **T — Tampering** | Attacker modifies data in transit or at rest | Integrity | Man-in-the-middle alters API request payload |
 11|| **R — Repudiation** | Attacker denies performing an action | Non-repudiation | User disputes a financial transaction with no audit trail |
 12|| **I — Information Disclosure** | Sensitive data exposed to unauthorized parties | Confidentiality | Error message leaks stack trace and database schema |
 13|| **D — Denial of Service** | System made unavailable to legitimate users | Availability | Unbounded API request floods Lambda concurrency |
 14|| **E — Elevation of Privilege** | Attacker gains higher access than authorized | Authorization | Regular user exploits IDOR to access admin endpoints |
 15|
 16|## Threat Modelling Process
 17|
 18|### Step 1: Define Scope
 19|Identify what you are threat-modelling: a single microservice, a complete feature, or an entire system. Smaller scopes produce more actionable results.
 20|
 21|### Step 2: Create a Data Flow Diagram (DFD)
 22|Draw the system showing:
 23|- **External entities**: Users, third-party systems, partner APIs
 24|- **Processes**: Lambda functions, ECS services, API Gateway
 25|- **Data stores**: DynamoDB tables, S3 buckets, RDS instances
 26|- **Data flows**: Arrows showing data movement, labelled with protocol and data type
 27|- **Trust boundaries**: Lines separating zones of different trust levels (public internet, VPC, private subnet)
 28|
 29|### Step 3: Identify Threats
 30|Walk through each element and data flow in the DFD. For each, ask the six STRIDE questions:
 31|- Can an attacker spoof this identity?
 32|- Can an attacker tamper with this data?
 33|- Can an attacker deny this action?
 34|- Can this component leak information?
 35|- Can this component be denied service?
 36|- Can an attacker elevate privilege through this component?
 37|
 38|### Step 4: Assess Risk
 39|For each identified threat, score it using likelihood and impact.
 40|
 41|### Step 5: Define Mitigations
 42|Map each threat to a specific countermeasure. Track mitigations as actionable tasks in the backlog.
 43|
 44|## Risk Scoring: Likelihood x Impact
 45|
 46|Use a simple 3x3 or 5x5 matrix:
 47|
 48|| | Low Impact | Medium Impact | High Impact |
 49||---|-----------|---------------|-------------|
 50|| **High Likelihood** | Medium | High | Critical |
 51|| **Medium Likelihood** | Low | Medium | High |
 52|| **Low Likelihood** | Low | Low | Medium |
 53|
 54|- **Likelihood factors**: Attack complexity, required access level, availability of exploits, attacker motivation.
 55|- **Impact factors**: Data sensitivity, financial loss, regulatory penalties, reputational damage, blast radius.
 56|
 57|## The DREAD Model (Alternative Scoring)
 58|
 59|Score each threat 1-10 on five dimensions, then average:
 60|- **Damage**: How severe is the impact?
 61|- **Reproducibility**: How reliably can the attack be repeated?
 62|- **Exploitability**: How much skill/effort is required?
 63|- **Affected Users**: How many users are impacted?
 64|- **Discoverability**: How easy is the vulnerability to find?
 65|
 66|DREAD is useful when STRIDE identifies many threats and you need to prioritize.
 67|
 68|## Attack Surface Analysis
 69|
 70|Enumerate all entry points an attacker could target:
 71|- Public API endpoints (API Gateway, ALB)
 72|- Authentication flows (Cognito hosted UI, custom login)
 73|- File upload endpoints (S3 pre-signed URLs)
 74|- WebSocket connections
 75|- Third-party integrations (webhooks, OAuth callbacks)
 76|- Administrative interfaces (console access, SSH, bastion)
 77|- CI/CD pipelines (build scripts, deployment credentials)
 78|
 79|Minimize attack surface: disable unused endpoints, restrict network access, apply least-privilege IAM.
 80|
 81|## Mitigation Mapping
 82|
 83|For each STRIDE category, common AWS mitigations include:
 84|
 85|| Category | Mitigations |
 86||----------|-------------|
 87|| Spoofing | Cognito + MFA, mutual TLS, API key rotation, IAM roles (no long-lived credentials) |
 88|| Tampering | HTTPS everywhere, S3 Object Lock, DynamoDB encryption, request signing |
 89|| Repudiation | CloudTrail logging, application audit logs, DynamoDB Streams for change history |
 90|| Information Disclosure | Encryption at rest (KMS), VPC endpoints, security groups, suppress verbose errors |
 91|| Denial of Service | WAF rate limiting, API Gateway throttling, Lambda reserved concurrency, Shield Advanced |
 92|| Elevation of Privilege | Least-privilege IAM, ABAC policies, input validation, IDOR checks in application logic |
 93|
 94|## When to Threat Model
 95|
 96|- During design (Stage 3 of AI-DLC) before implementation begins.
 97|- When adding a new external integration or data flow.
 98|- When changing authentication or authorization mechanisms.
 99|- After a security incident, to update the model with newly discovered threats.
100|- Review and refresh threat models at least annually.
</file-view>

 47|# Build and Test
 48|
 49|## Steps
 50|
 51|### Step 1: Analyze Testing Requirements
 52|
 53|Read code generation outputs across all units from
 54|`<record>/construction/*/code-generation/code-summary.md` and per-unit test
 55|instructions from
 56|`<record>/construction/*/code-generation/unit-test-instructions.md`. For a
 57|zero-Unit scope such as `express`, read the stage-level equivalents under
 58|`<record>/construction/code-generation/`.
 59|
 60|Build a source-complete inventory of every measurable quality target before
 61|generating instructions. Read all applicable stage-level and per-unit sources:
 62|
 63|- every artifact under `nfr-requirements/`
 64|- every artifact under `nfr-design/`
 65|- every approved `## Testing Contract` in `code-generation-plan.md`
 66|
 67|For each target, record a stable target ID (derive one from the source path and
 68|section when the source has none), source path/section, expected value, the
 69|check or instruction file that will produce its actual value, and the later
 70|validation stage that owns it when Build and Test cannot execute it locally.
 71|Catalog all required test types from this inventory.
 72|
 73|### Step 2: Generate Build Instructions
 74|
 75|Create `<record>/construction/build-and-test/build-instructions.md`:
 76|- Dependency installation steps
 77|- Environment setup (env vars, config files, local services)
 78|- Build commands (compile, bundle, transpile)
 79|- Build verification steps
 80|- Troubleshooting common build issues
 81|
 82|### Step 3-7: Generate Test Instructions (Strategy-Aware)
 83|
 84|Consult the active test strategy from `aidlc-state.md` → `**Test Strategy**` (see stage-protocol.md §8 "Test Strategy"). Generate additional test instruction files based on the strategy level:
 85|
 86|**Minimal strategy** — generate no additional test instruction files. Unit
 87|tests are covered per-unit by Code Generation.
 88|
 89|**Standard strategy** — generate:
 90|- `integration-test-instructions.md`: Key boundary tests, cross-unit interaction
 91|
 92|**Comprehensive strategy** — generate all applicable:
 93|- `integration-test-instructions.md`: Cross-unit interaction, external dependency handling
 94|- `performance-test-instructions.md` (IF NFR performance requirements exist): Load testing, benchmarks, regression detection
 95|- `security-test-instructions.md` (IF NFR security requirements exist): SAST/DAST, auth testing, injection testing
 96|- Additional types as applicable (contract tests, E2E, accessibility) — create specifically named files
 97|
 98|All files go in `<record>/construction/build-and-test/`.
 99|
100|Each instruction file should include:
101|- Test framework setup and configuration
102|- How to run the tests (commands, flags, filters)
103|- Expected coverage targets appropriate to the strategy level
104|- Test data management and environment setup
105|
106|These are soft guidelines — the LLM can generate additional test types at any strategy level if context demands it (e.g., a Minimal security-patch may still warrant security test instructions).
107|
108|### Step 8: Generate Build and Test Summary
109|
110|Create `<record>/construction/build-and-test/build-and-test-summary.md`:
111|- Overall build status and prerequisites
112|- Test type inventory (which test types were generated)
113|- Coverage expectations per unit
114|- A `## Target Verification Matrix` with one row per target and these columns:
115|  Target ID, Source, Expected, Actual, Evidence, Owning Stage, Verdict
116|- Each applicable target begins with Actual and Evidence `Pending`, and Verdict
117|  `Pending`. `N/A` is valid only when the source inventory found no applicable
118|  measurable target; in that case write one explanatory `N/A` row. An
119|  applicable target may never use `N/A`.
120|- Readiness assessment (build-ready, test-ready, deployment-ready)
121|- Known limitations or outstanding items
122|
123|### Step 9: Execute Build and Tests
124|
125|Attempt to execute the build and test commands documented in the instruction files:
126|
127|1. **Build**: Run the build commands from `build-instructions.md` via Bash. Capture output.
128|2. **Unit tests**: Collect the run commands from both the stage-level
129|   `<record>/construction/code-generation/unit-test-instructions.md` file (when
130|   present, including Express) and all per-unit
131|   `<record>/construction/*/code-generation/unit-test-instructions.md` files.
132|   Deduplicate identical commands and run each distinct command ONCE via Bash.
133|   Per-unit commands should already be scoped to their Unit. A stage-level or
134|   malformed per-unit file may carry a project-wide command; run that command
135|   once, never N times. Capture and report stage-level/per-unit pass/fail
136|   results without double counting.
137|3. **Integration tests** (if applicable): Run integration test commands. Capture results.
138|4. **Other applicable checks**: Run every applicable command from performance,
139|   security, contract, E2E, accessibility, and other generated instruction
140|   files. A check may be deferred only when it requires a deployed or
141|   production-like environment AND the current execution plan contains a later
142|   validation stage that explicitly owns that check (for example,
143|   `performance-validation`). Record the owning stage and expected evidence
144|   path. A deferred target remains `Unverified` and cannot contribute to a
145|   successful stage result. If no later owning stage is scheduled, the target
146|   is `Unverified`, not deferred successfully.
147|5. **Finalize and report results**: Create or update
148|   `<record>/construction/build-and-test/test-results.md` and the Build and Test
149|   Summary on every exit path, including loop-back, halt-and-ask, abort, and
150|   accepted failure, with:
151|   - Build status (success/failure + output)
152|   - Test results (total, passed, failed, skipped)
153|   - Failure details (test name, assertion, stack trace)
154|   - Coverage report (if test framework supports it)
155|   - The finalized Target Verification Matrix: actual value, evidence path or
156|     command output, owning stage, and exactly one final verdict per applicable
157|     target: `Met`, `Not Met`, or `Unverified`. `Pending` is allowed only while
158|     Step 8 is being prepared; no `Pending` verdict may remain when Step 9
159|     exits.
160|   - `## Loop-Back Log` (only when the failure ladder's rung 3 or 4 fires a
161|     loop-back): one `### Loop-back N — <ISO timestamp>` entry per attempt,
162|     carrying Diagnosis / Root-cause stage / Planned fix / Estimated impact. This section
163|     is APPEND-ONLY and must survive re-runs of this stage (choose Modify,
164|     never Redo, on loop-back re-entry — Redo would erase the ledger).
165|
166|**Failure predicate**: Build and Test has failed when any build or test command
167|fails OR any applicable target is `Not Met` or `Unverified`. Before entering
168|failure handling, finalize the matrix and summary with all evidence available
169|on that exit path. Weakening, relaxing, lowering, or disabling a defined
170|quality target is never an acceptable fix.
171|
172|**On failure**: Run the same failure-escalation ladder for command failures,
173|`Not Met` targets, and `Unverified` targets:
174|
175|1. **In-stage fix (max 2 attempts)** — for root causes inside this stage's own
176|   remit (test config, build scripts, environment setup, or an executable target
177|   check): read the failure evidence, identify the failing configuration or
178|   scaffolding, apply the fix, re-run the failing step, and refresh the target
179|   matrix.
180|2. **Classify and estimate impact** — when in-stage attempts are exhausted OR the
181|   diagnosis points upstream: decide whether the root cause lies in the
182|   generated source or test code — regardless of defect size — or an approach
183|   chosen at code-generation (library/version, container image, instance type,
184|   algorithm, flag). If so, look for an identifiable fix in a swappable
185|   dimension (newer image, driver, wheel index, a CLI flag) and ESTIMATE ITS
186|   IMPACT — effort, financial cost, risk. Never declare a feasible path out of

- Python 3 on `PATH` (`python3 --version` should succeed). No third-party
  dependencies — standard library only (NFR1).

## Dependency Installation

None. The project uses only the Python 3 standard library; there is no
`requirements.txt`, package manifest, or virtualenv to create.

## Environment Setup

None. No environment variables, config files, or local services are

 17|# Pipeline & Deploy Agent
 18|
 19|You are a senior CI/CD engineer and release manager specializing in continuous integration pipeline design, deployment strategy, and release execution. You translate build specifications and infrastructure targets into fully automated pipelines that take code from commit to production with quality gates, rollback safety, and full auditability. You have Bash access for running pipeline tools, deployment scripts, and smoke test commands.
 20|
 21|## Core Responsibilities
 22|
 23|### CI Pipeline Configuration
 24|- Design and configure CI pipelines for each buildable component (lint, build, unit test, integration test, security scan)
 25|- Define pipeline triggers (push, PR, schedule, tag) and branch strategies
 26|- Configure artifact generation, versioning, and registry publication
 27|- Implement build caching and parallelization for fast feedback cycles
 28|- Define quality gates that block promotion on test failure, coverage regression, or vulnerability detection
 29|
 30|### Deployment Pipeline Design
 31|- Design CD pipelines that promote artifacts through environment tiers (dev, staging, production)
 32|- Select deployment strategies per component (blue-green, canary, rolling, recreate)
 33|- Implement promotion gates (automated test pass, manual approval, canary metric thresholds)
 34|- Configure feature flag integration for progressive delivery and dark launches
 35|- Define database migration execution within deployment pipelines (forward-only, backward-compatible)
 36|
 37|### Deployment Execution & Release
 38|- Execute deployments to target environments using infrastructure-as-code outputs
 39|- Run pre-deployment validation checks (environment health, dependency availability)
 40|- Execute smoke tests and synthetic monitors post-deployment
 41|- Monitor deployment health metrics during canary or rolling rollouts
 42|- Execute rollback procedures when deployment health checks fail
 43|
 44|### Rollback & Recovery Procedures
 45|- Define rollback triggers (health check failure, error rate spike, latency breach)
 46|- Implement automated rollback with configurable thresholds and cooldown periods
 47|- Design database rollback strategies that maintain data integrity
 48|- Document manual recovery procedures for scenarios beyond automated rollback
 49|- Conduct post-rollback analysis to identify root cause and prevent recurrence
 50|
 51|### Artifact & Release Management
 52|- Define artifact naming, versioning, and tagging conventions (semver, git SHA, build number)
 53|- Configure artifact repositories (container registry, package repository, S3 buckets)
 54|- Manage release notes generation from commit history and changelog entries
 55|- Define artifact retention policies and cleanup automation
 56|- Track artifact provenance from source commit through deployment
 57|
 58|### Worktree Branch Lifecycle (orchestrator-dispatched at Bolt boundaries)
 59|- Receive create / merge / discard dispatches from the orchestrator at Bolt boundaries (SKILL.md per-Bolt execution: pre-`BOLT_STARTED` create, post-`BOLT_COMPLETED` merge)
 60|- Read `## Way of Working` from `aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/{project,team,org}.md` per `.devin/knowledge/aidlc-shared/rules-reading.md`; match the affirmed branching strategy to one of the five in `branching-strategies.md`
 61|- Resolve `aidlc-worktree` flags (`--slug`, `--base`, `--target`, `--strategy`, optional `--message`) per the chosen strategy's runbook
 62|- Invoke `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree` from the main repo checkout; `aidlc-worktree` itself emits the audit event audit-first before invoking git

 64|- On conflict envelopes, do not retry — return the envelope and let the orchestrator's halt-and-ask offer the user retry/abort/discard. On retry/abort, the orchestrator's halt-and-ask preserves the worktree at the path returned in the conflict envelope.
 65|- Worktree work is orchestrator-dispatched and not anchored to a single Stages-Owned entry; same dispatch pattern as how the orchestrator dispatches `developer-agent` for code generation today
 66|
 67|## Collaboration
 68|
 69|- **Receives from**: Developer Agent (buildable source, test suites, build scripts), Quality Agent (test requirements, quality gate definitions), AWS Platform Agent (environment endpoints, infrastructure outputs)
 70|- **Works with**: Developer Agent (build configuration, dependency resolution), Quality Agent (test integration into pipelines, quality gate thresholds), AWS Platform Agent (deployment targets, environment variables, secrets)
 71|- **Hands off to**: Operations Agent (deployed services for observability setup), Quality Agent (deployment artifacts for performance validation)
 72|
 73|## Memory Focus
 74|
 75|`aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/{org,team,project}.md` -- active-space guardrails and affirmed practices (read per `.devin/knowledge/aidlc-shared/rules-reading.md`). Consult `## Way of Working`, `## Deployment`, and `## Testing Posture` when selecting branch, release, and gate behavior.
 76|
 77|## Key Principles
 78|
 79|1. **Every commit is a release candidate** -- The pipeline must treat every commit as potentially deployable. If it passes all gates, it is ready for production.
 80|2. **Rollback is not optional** -- Every deployment must have a tested rollback path. A deployment without rollback capability is a deployment without a safety net.
 81|3. **Fast pipelines, fast feedback** -- CI pipelines should complete in minutes, not hours. Slow pipelines encourage batching, and batching increases risk.
 82|4. **Gates protect production** -- Quality gates exist to prevent defective artifacts from reaching users. Bypassing a gate is an incident, not a shortcut.
 83|5. **Automate the ceremony** -- Release notes, changelogs, version bumps, and notifications should be automated. Manual release ceremonies introduce human error and delay.
 84|6. **Deployment is not done until smoke passes** -- A successful deployment is not a successful deploy command. It is a deployment where smoke tests confirm the service is healthy in its new environment.

  1|# Branching Strategies
  2|
  3|A menu of common branching strategies, what they look like, when to use them, and how AIDLC's Construction worktrees map onto each. When the orchestrator dispatches aidlc-pipeline-deploy-agent at Bolt boundaries, this file is the menu the agent surveys to map a team's affirmed branching strategy onto the `aidlc-worktree` tool's flags.
  4|
  5|> **Reading practices:** see `knowledge/aidlc-shared/rules-reading.md` for empty-template detection, semantic-topic matching, and the active-space `project.md → team.md → org.md → hardcoded defaults` fallback chain. In the runbooks below, those files live under `aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/`.
  6|>
  7|> See also `cicd-patterns.md` § "Branch Strategies" for the higher-level CI-flow context.
  8|
  9|---
 10|
 11|## Trunk-Based Development (default)
 12|
 13|```
 14|main ────────────────────────────────────────►
 15|  ▲   ▲   ▲   ▲   ▲   ▲
 16|  │   │   │   │   │   │   short-lived feature branches
 17|  │   │   │   │   │   │   (1-2 days max), squash-merge to main
 18|  bolt-1  bolt-3      bolt-5
 19|      bolt-2  bolt-4
 20|```
 21|
 22|**Shape.** All work merges to `main` via short-lived feature branches. Long-lived branches don't exist. Feature flags gate incomplete work in production.
 23|
 24|**When to use.** Default for most teams. Especially when CI pipeline duration is short (under 30 minutes) and observability is good enough to detect production issues quickly.
 25|
 26|**Common problems.**
 27|- Teams with infrequent releases find it hard to "hold" features for a release window. Feature flags are the answer, not branches.
 28|- Teams without good test coverage shouldn't trunk-base — every commit hits production-shaped pipelines, so flaky tests block everyone.
 29|
 30|**Worktree mapping.** Create: `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree create --slug <bolt-slug> --base main`. Merge: `--target main --strategy squash`. Each Bolt = one squash commit on `main`.
 31|
 32|**Parallel Bolts.** Cleanest fit. Multiple Bolts can be in flight simultaneously; each branches from current `main`, each merges back without rebase contention because squash flattens history at merge time.
 33|
 34|### Execution runbook
 35|
 36|When dispatched for trunk-based:
 37|
 38|1. Read `## Way of Working` from the active space's `project.md`, `team.md`, then `org.md` per `shared/rules-reading.md`; use hardcoded defaults only if all three are empty.
 39|2. Resolve flags: `--base main --target main --strategy squash` for the default; deviate only if `team.md` explicitly says otherwise.
 40|3. **Create**: invoke `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree create --slug <bolt-slug> --base main`.
 41|4. **Merge** (after Bolt gate approval): caller must be on `main` at the main checkout. Invoke `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree merge --slug <bolt-slug> --target main --strategy squash --message "<commit message>"`.
 42|5. Return the JSON envelope per § Response contract back to the orchestrator.
 43|
 44|### Failure modes
 45|
 46|- **Dirty tree on merge.** Local uncommitted changes on `main`; tool errors with the git message verbatim. Orchestrator's halt-and-ask offers retry/abort. Worktree preserved on retry; user explicitly discards on abort.
 47|- **Conflict on squash.** Squash conflicts with concurrent `main` motion (e.g. another Bolt landed first). Tool exits non-zero with `{status: "conflict", conflict_files, detail}`. Orchestrator quotes `detail` to the user.
 48|- **Branch already exists.** Pre-audit error; the tool refuses to clobber. Orchestrator should run `discard` first (rare) or pick a different slug.
 49|
 50|---
 51|
 52|## GitHub Flow
 53|
 54|```
 55|main ────────────────────────────────────────►
 56|  ▲       ▲       ▲       ▲
 57|  │       │       │       │   feature branches with PRs
 58|  │       │       │       │   (no time limit; can live longer than 1-2 days)
 59|  feat-A  feat-B  feat-C  feat-D
 60|```
 61|
 62|**Shape.** `main` + indefinite feature branches. PRs merge to `main`. Branches can live longer than trunk-based — days to weeks for larger features. No `develop` or `release` branches.
 63|
 64|**When to use.** Teams that want trunk-based discipline but need longer-lived feature branches. Open-source projects often use this.
 65|
 66|**Common problems.**
 67|- Branches that live too long accumulate merge debt. Discipline required to either land or close.
 68|- Without feature flags, in-flight features block release of unrelated work.
 69|
 70|**Worktree mapping.** Same base/target as trunk-based: `--base main --target main`. Strategy is usually `squash`, but teams that prefer to preserve the branch in history use `merge`. Team picks at affirmation; agent reads `team.md`.
 71|
 72|### Execution runbook
 73|
 74|When dispatched for GitHub Flow:
 75|
 76|1. Read `## Way of Working` from the active space's `project.md`, `team.md`, then `org.md` (including any merge-style statement). The merge-strategy choice (squash vs merge) is what differs from trunk-based.
 77|2. Resolve flags: `--base main --target main --strategy <squash|merge>` per affirmation; default to `squash`.
 78|3. **Create**: `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree create --slug <bolt-slug> --base main`.
 79|4. **Merge**: `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree merge --slug <bolt-slug> --target main --strategy <squash|merge> [--message "<msg>"]`. With `--strategy merge`, a no-fast-forward merge commit preserves the bolt branch's individual commits.
 80|5. Return per § Response contract.
 81|
 82|### Failure modes
 83|
 84|- **Same as trunk-based**, plus:
 85|- **Stale base for `--strategy merge`.** Long-lived bolt branches against a moving `main` produce conflicts. The tool reports the conflict envelope; the user resolves in the worktree (preserved on conflict) and re-invokes merge.
 86|
 87|---
 88|
 89|## GitFlow
 90|
 91|```
 92|main         ────────────────────────────────►
 93|              ▲           ▲
 94|              │           │   release/v1.0   release/v1.1
 95|develop ─────┴───────────┴────────────────────►
 96|  ▲   ▲   ▲       ▲   ▲
 97|  │   │   │       │   │       feature branches off develop
 98|  │   │   │       │   │
 99|  feat-A feat-B   feat-C feat-D
100|                    ▲
101|                    │ hotfix/v1.0.1 (off main, merged to both)
102|```
103|
104|**Shape.** Two long-lived branches (`main` = production, `develop` = integration), plus `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*` short-lived branches. Releases cut from `develop` → `release/*` → `main` with version tags.
105|
106|**When to use.** Teams with strict release management — quarterly releases, regulated deployments, stable production while integration continues. Common in enterprise + financial services.
107|
108|**Common problems.**
109|- Long-lived `develop` accumulates merge debt against `main` over a release cycle. Painful merges at release-cut time.
110|- Hotfixes require dual-merging (to both `main` and `develop`) — easy to miss the second merge.
111|
112|**Worktree mapping.** Feature Bolts: `--base develop --target develop`. Hotfix Bolts: `--base main --target main` (and the operator merges to `develop` separately — out of scope for `aidlc-worktree`). Strategy is usually `merge` to preserve branch history; `squash` is also valid.
113|
114|### Execution runbook
115|
116|When dispatched for GitFlow:
117|
118|1. Read the active space's `## Way of Working`. Look for the integration-branch name (`develop` is the convention; teams sometimes use `integration` or `next`).
119|2. For feature Bolts: `--base <integration> --target <integration> --strategy <merge|squash>`. Default to `merge`.
120|3. For hotfix Bolts (rare in Construction; usually triggered by an out-of-band stage): `--base main --target main --strategy merge`. The operator separately merges the hotfix back to `<integration>` after `aidlc-worktree merge` succeeds. Out of scope for the tool.
121|4. **Create**: `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree create --slug <bolt-slug> --base <integration>`.
122|5. **Merge**: caller must be on `<integration>` at the main checkout. `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree merge --slug <bolt-slug> --target <integration> --strategy <merge|squash>`.
123|6. Return per § Response contract; if hotfix, include `notes: "manual merge to <integration> required"` so the orchestrator surfaces the follow-up.
124|
125|### Failure modes
126|
127|- **`<integration>` branch missing locally.** Pre-audit error; tool refuses to invent the branch.
128|- **Wrong cwd on merge.** Defensive HEAD check fails: `expected branch <integration>, found <actual>`. Caller must `cd` to the main checkout and `git checkout <integration>` first.
129|- **Hotfix merge to second target forgotten.** Out-of-scope for `aidlc-worktree`; orchestrator's aidlc-pipeline-deploy-agent dispatch should always include the second-target reminder in `notes`.
130|
131|---
132|
133|## Release Branches
134|
135|```
136|main         ────────────────────────────────►
137|              ▲                       ▲
138|              │                       │
139|release/v1.0 ┴──── (frozen for stabilisation) ──────►
140|  ▲   ▲
141|  │   │   bug fixes only on release branch
142|  │   │
143|  fix-A fix-B
144|              │
145|              └──► merge release/v1.0 → main + tag v1.0.0
146|```
147|
148|**Shape.** Trunk-based or GitHub Flow on `main`, with a release branch cut at code-freeze. Stabilisation work (bug fixes only) happens on the release branch; new features continue on `main`.
149|
150|**When to use.** Teams shipping versioned software where release stability matters more than continuous deployment — desktop apps, embedded software, enterprise products with hard release dates.
151|
152|**Common problems.**
153|- Bug fixes on release branch must be cherry-picked or merged back to `main` so they don't regress in the next release.
154|- Long stabilisation periods can block feature work waiting for the release branch to merge back.
155|
156|**Worktree mapping.** Bolts on `main` use `--base main --target main`. Release-branch fix Bolts use `--base release/vX.Y --target release/vX.Y`. Strategy is `merge` typically (preserves the fix branch in history for traceability).
157|
158|### Execution runbook
159|
160|When dispatched for Release Branches:
161|
162|1. Read the active space's `## Way of Working`. Look for the release-branch pattern (`release/vX.Y` is the convention).
163|2. Determine which line the Bolt belongs to from the Bolt's metadata (the orchestrator passes a `target_line: main | release/vX.Y` hint). Default to `main` when ambiguous.
164|3. **Create**: `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree create --slug <bolt-slug> --base <line>`.
165|4. **Merge**: caller on `<line>` at the main checkout. `bun .devin/tools/aidlc.ts engine worktree merge --slug <bolt-slug> --target <line> --strategy merge`.
166|5. If the Bolt was a release-branch fix, include `notes: "consider cherry-pick to main"` in the response — the operator handles the cross-merge.
167|6. Return per § Response contract.
168|
169|### Failure modes
170|
171|- **Release branch missing locally.** Pre-audit error.
172|- **Bolt targeted release branch but main has diverged.** Bolt completes; orchestrator surfaces the cherry-pick reminder via the `notes` field.
173|- **Same as GitFlow** for wrong-cwd / dirty-tree / conflict cases.
174|
175|---
176|
177|## Monorepo
178|
179|```
180|main ────────────────────────────────────────►
181|  ▲   ▲   ▲   ▲
182|  │   │   │   │   feature branches with path-based scope
183|  │   │   │   │
184|  pkg-a/feat-1  pkg-b/feat-2  pkg-c/refactor  shared/lib-update
185|```
186|
187|**Shape.** Single repo holding multiple packages/services. Branches scoped by path (changes within `packages/auth/` are one Bolt; changes spanning packages need explicit cross-package coordination). Can run trunk-based, GitHub Flow, or any of the above on top.
188|
189|**When to use.** Teams with multiple closely-coupled services that benefit from atomic cross-service changes. Tooling support required: Nx, Turborepo, Pants.
190|
191|**Common problems.**
192|- CI must be path-aware (only test packages with changes). Monolithic CI defeats the purpose.
193|- Cross-package changes can't be parallelised cleanly — they require coordinated merges.
194|
195|**Worktree mapping.** Same as the underlying strategy (trunk-based default). The path-awareness lives at the CI/test layer, not the worktree layer. Strategy is usually `squash` per package change.
196|
197|### Execution runbook
198|
199|When dispatched for Monorepo:
200|
201|1. Resolve the underlying strategy (trunk-based default) per its runbook above.
202|2. The Bolt slug should encode the package scope (e.g. `auth-token-rotation` rather than `feature-1`) so `git worktree list` output stays diagnosable.
203|3. Create + merge identical to the underlying strategy.
204|4. Return per § Response contract.
205|
206|### Failure modes
207|
208|- **Cross-package Bolts.** When a Bolt's units span two packages, the merge succeeds but the cherry-pick / coordinate-with-other-package reminder is the operator's job. Surface in `notes` if known.
209|- **Same as the underlying strategy.**
210|
211|---
212|
213|## Response contract
214|
215|When the orchestrator dispatches aidlc-pipeline-deploy-agent for a worktree create or merge, the agent invokes `aidlc-worktree` directly and reports the JSON envelope below back to the orchestrator. SKILL.md Step 0.5 / Step 6.75 then call `aidlc-worktree verify` as a deterministic backstop confirming the audit event landed.
216|
217|### Create response (success)
218|
219|```json
220|{
221|  "emitted": "WORKTREE_CREATED",
222|  "slug": "<bolt-slug>",
223|  "worktree_path": "/abs/path/.aidlc/worktrees/bolt-<slug>",
224|  "branch": "bolt-<slug>",
225|  "base": "<base-branch>",
226|  "audit_timestamp": "2026-05-18T12:34:56Z",
227|  "notes": "<optional follow-up reminders for the orchestrator>"
228|}
229|```
230|
231|### Merge response (success)
232|
233|```json
234|{
235|  "emitted": "WORKTREE_MERGED",
236|  "slug": "<bolt-slug>",
237|  "worktree_path": "/abs/path/.aidlc/worktrees/bolt-<slug>",
238|  "target": "<target-branch>",
239|  "strategy": "squash",
240|  "commit_sha": "<sha>",
241|  "audit_timestamp": "2026-05-18T12:34:56Z",
242|  "notes": "<optional follow-up reminders>"
243|}
244|```
245|
246|If a merge error carries `[merge-succeeded:<sha>]` and says the
247|`SWARM_SOURCE_MERGED` post-result audit row failed, the Git merge already
248|landed but no aggregate source authority exists. Preserve the worktree and do
249|not retry the same merge command. Restart the stage attempt, or use
250|`AIDLC_SKIP_SOURCE_FRESHNESS=1` only after explicit human approval.
251|
252|### Merge response (conflict)
253|
254|```json
255|{
256|  "status": "conflict",
257|  "slug": "<bolt-slug>",
258|  "worktree_path": "/abs/path/.aidlc/worktrees/bolt-<slug>",
259|  "conflict_files": ["src/foo.ts", "src/bar.ts"],
260|  "detail": "Merge produced conflicts in worktree at <path>. Worktree preserved for inspection."
261|}
262|```
263|
264|The orchestrator's halt-and-ask quotes the `detail` field verbatim. See `aidlc-common/protocols/stage-protocol-construction.md` § "Halt-and-ask on failure" and `skills/aidlc/SKILL.md` § "Halt-and-ask failure handling" for the full prompt shape and preservation invariant.
265|
266|### Discard response
267|
268|```json
269|{
270|  "emitted": "WORKTREE_DISCARDED",
271|  "slug": "<bolt-slug>",
272|  "worktree_path": "/abs/path/.aidlc/worktrees/bolt-<slug>",
273|  "reason": "agent-discard",
274|  "audit_timestamp": "2026-05-18T12:34:56Z"
275|}
276|```
277|
278|If the worktree was already gone (idempotent path), `emitted` is `null` and `reason` is `already-discarded` — no audit event is re-emitted.
279|
280|---
281|
282|## How AIDLC reads strategy from team practices
283|
284|The dispatch protocol described in this section is implemented by **SKILL.md Step 0** (worktree create) and **Step 6.5** (worktree merge). `aidlc-bolt complete --merge` orchestrates around the dispatch (forkState merge-back, forkAudit merge-back) but does not call `aidlc-worktree merge` directly — the dispatch lives in SKILL.md prose.
285|
286|When a Bolt starts (Step 0) or completes (Step 6.5), the orchestrator dispatches a Task call to **aidlc-pipeline-deploy-agent** with two inputs:
287|
288|1. The resolved `## Way of Working` statement from `aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/{project,team,org}.md` (fallback chain in `shared/rules-reading.md`).
289|2. The Bolt's metadata (slug, source branch, optional target-line hint for release-branch teams).
290|
291|The agent reads this file (`branching-strategies.md`) as the menu, matches the team's stated strategy to one of the five above, picks the right `aidlc-worktree` flags, invokes the tool, and returns the response envelope per § Response contract.
292|
293|If the team's stated strategy doesn't map cleanly to the menu (e.g. "we use a hybrid"), the agent picks the closest fit and notes the deviation in the response's `notes` field; the orchestrator surfaces it in the audit log.
294|
295|If none of `project.md`, `team.md`, or `org.md` provides a branching practice, the agent applies hardcoded defaults — trunk-based with squash, base `main`, target `main` — and emits `PRACTICES_SECTION_EMPTY` (advisory-only).
296|
297|---
298|
299|## Quick decision matrix
300|
301|| You want... | Use |
302||---|---|
303|| Default for a new project | Trunk-Based |
304|| OSS-style PRs with longer-lived branches | GitHub Flow |
305|| Enterprise release management | GitFlow |
306|| Versioned releases with stabilisation periods | Release Branches |
307|| Multiple services in one repo | Monorepo (on top of one of the above) |
308|
309|If unsure, choose Trunk-Based. It's the lowest-overhead strategy with the strongest CI/CD ecosystem support, and AIDLC's Construction worktrees are designed for it as the default.
</file-view>

  1|# CI/CD Pipeline Patterns
  2|
  3|Patterns for building reliable continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines.
  4|
  5|## CI Pipeline Stages
  6|
  7|A well-structured CI pipeline runs these stages in order:
  8|
  9|1. **Lint** — Code formatting and style checks (ESLint, Prettier, Ruff, Black). Catch trivial issues before deeper analysis. Fast (< 30 seconds).
 10|2. **Build** — Compile, transpile, or bundle the application. Verify the code produces valid artifacts. For CDK: `cdk synth`.
 11|3. **Unit Test** — Run fast, isolated tests. Target: < 3 minutes. Fail the pipeline on any test failure.
 12|4. **Static Analysis / Security Scan** — SAST, IaC scanning, dependency audit. Report findings; gate on severity thresholds.
 13|5. **Integration Test** — Test against real dependencies (databases, queues) using testcontainers or LocalStack. Target: < 10 minutes.
 14|6. **Package** — Build deployable artifacts: Docker images, Lambda ZIPs, CloudFormation templates. Tag with commit SHA and semantic version.
 15|
 16|## CD Pipeline Patterns
 17|
 18|### Continuous Delivery
 19|Every commit that passes CI is deployable, but a human triggers the production deployment. Use manual approval gates in CodePipeline or GitHub Actions environments.
 20|
 21|### Continuous Deployment
 22|Every commit that passes CI and staging validation deploys to production automatically. Requires high confidence in test coverage and automated rollback.
 23|
 24|**Recommendation**: Start with continuous delivery. Graduate to continuous deployment as test maturity and observability improve.
 25|
 26|## Branch Strategies
 27|
 28|> See `branching-strategies.md` in this directory for the deeper menu aidlc-pipeline-deploy-agent surveys at Bolt-merge dispatch — including diagrams, common problems, AIDLC worktree mapping per strategy, and parallel-Bolts notes for each. The summaries below cover the CI-flow context.
 29|
 30|### Trunk-Based Development (Preferred)
 31|- All developers commit to `main` (or short-lived feature branches merged within 1-2 days).
 32|- Feature flags gate incomplete work. No long-lived branches.
 33|- CI runs on every push to main. CD deploys from main.
 34|- Benefits: Fewer merge conflicts, faster feedback, simpler pipeline.
 35|
 36|### GitFlow
 37|- `main` (production), `develop` (integration), `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`.
 38|- Suitable for teams with infrequent releases or strict release management.
 39|- Drawback: Long-lived branches cause painful merges and delayed integration.
 40|
 41|### GitHub Flow
 42|- `main` + short-lived feature branches. PRs merge to main.
 43|- Simpler than GitFlow but still relies on branching. Good middle ground.
 44|
 45|## Quality Gates
 46|
 47|Define explicit pass/fail criteria that block pipeline progression:
 48|
 49|| Gate | Criteria | Stage |
 50||------|----------|-------|
 51|| Lint | Zero lint errors | Pre-build |
 52|| Test coverage | >= 80% line coverage, no decrease | Post-test |
 53|| Security scan | Zero Critical/High findings | Post-scan |
 54|| Integration tests | 100% pass rate | Post-integration |
 55|| Manual approval | Tech lead or product owner sign-off | Pre-production |
 56|| Smoke tests | Critical path tests pass in production | Post-deploy |
 57|
 58|## Artifact Management
 59|
 60|- **Amazon ECR**: Store Docker images. Use immutable tags (commit SHA), not `latest`.
 61|- **AWS CodeArtifact**: Host npm, pip, Maven packages. Proxy upstream registries for caching and security.
 62|- **S3**: Store Lambda deployment ZIPs, CloudFormation templates, and build outputs.
 63|- Tag every artifact with: commit SHA, build number, branch, timestamp.
 64|- Set lifecycle policies: keep the last 30 tagged images; expire untagged images after 7 days.
 65|
 66|## Pipeline as Code
 67|
 68|- Define pipelines in version-controlled files, not UI configurations.
 69|- **GitHub Actions**: `.github/workflows/*.yml`. Matrix builds for multi-version testing.
 70|- **AWS CodePipeline + CodeBuild**: `buildspec.yml` for build steps; pipeline defined in CDK or CloudFormation.
 71|- **Reusable workflows**: Extract common steps (lint, test, deploy) into shared workflow templates. Avoid copy-paste across repos.
 72|
 73|## Monorepo vs Polyrepo CI Strategies
 74|
 75|### Monorepo
 76|- Use path-based triggers: only build/test services whose files changed.
 77|- Tools: Nx, Turborepo, Pants. These understand dependency graphs and skip unchanged packages.
 78|- Shared CI steps (lint, security scan) run once; service-specific steps run conditionally.
 79|
 80|### Polyrepo
 81|- Each repo has its own pipeline. Simpler per-repo but harder to coordinate cross-service changes.
 82|- Use contract testing (Pact) to verify compatibility across repos without a monolithic integration test.
 83|- Automate dependency updates across repos with Renovate or a custom bot.
 84|
 85|## Pipeline Performance
 86|
 87|- Target: commit to production in under 30 minutes (excluding manual approval).
 88|- Parallelize independent stages (lint + unit test, SAST + dependency scan).
 89|- Cache dependencies aggressively (npm cache, pip cache, Docker layer caching).
 90|- Use spot instances or reserved capacity for build workers to reduce cost.
 91|- Monitor pipeline duration as a team metric; alert when it exceeds thresholds.
</file-view>

  1|# Deployment Strategies
  2|
  3|Patterns for releasing software safely with minimal risk to users and the ability to roll back quickly.
  4|
  5|## Blue/Green Deployment
  6|
  7|**How it works**: Maintain two identical environments (blue = current, green = new). Deploy the new version to green. Switch traffic from blue to green at the load balancer or DNS level. Keep blue running as an instant rollback target.
  8|
  9|**AWS Implementation**:
 10|- ECS: Use CodeDeploy with `ECS` deployment type. Two target groups on an ALB; CodeDeploy shifts traffic.
 11|- Lambda: Use aliases with weighted traffic shifting (`AWS::Lambda::Alias` with `RoutingConfig`).
 12|- Elastic Beanstalk: Swap environment URLs.
 13|
 14|**Advantages**: Instant rollback (repoint to blue), full environment validation before switch.
 15|**Drawbacks**: Double infrastructure cost during deployment window. Database schema must be backward-compatible.
 16|
 17|## Canary Releases
 18|
 19|**How it works**: Route a small percentage of traffic (1-5%) to the new version. Monitor error rates, latency, and business metrics. Gradually increase traffic if healthy; roll back if anomalies are detected.
 20|
 21|**AWS Implementation**:
 22|- CodeDeploy with Lambda or ECS: Built-in canary configurations (`Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery1Minute`).
 23|- API Gateway: Canary release on stage with percentage-based traffic split.
 24|- CloudWatch alarms trigger automatic rollback on metric breaches.
 25|
 26|**Advantages**: Limits blast radius. Detects issues with real traffic before full rollout.
 27|**Drawbacks**: Requires robust monitoring. Stateful services need careful handling.
 28|
 29|## Rolling Updates
 30|
 31|**How it works**: Replace instances/tasks in batches. New version replaces a subset while the rest continue serving. Repeat until all instances run the new version.
 32|
 33|**AWS Implementation**:
 34|- ECS: Default deployment strategy. Configure `minimumHealthyPercent` and `maximumPercent`.
 35|- EC2 Auto Scaling: Rolling update policy with `MinInstancesInService`.
 36|
 37|**Advantages**: No extra infrastructure cost. Gradual rollout.
 38|**Drawbacks**: Mixed versions during deployment (ensure backward compatibility). Slower rollback (redeploy the previous version).
 39|
 40|## A/B Testing
 41|
 42|**How it works**: Route specific user segments to different versions based on attributes (user ID, region, account type). Measure business outcomes (conversion, engagement) to decide which version wins.
 43|
 44|**Distinction from canary**: A/B testing serves different experiences intentionally for experimentation; canary is a deployment safety mechanism.
 45|
 46|**AWS Implementation**: CloudWatch Evidently for feature experiments with statistical analysis. CloudFront + Lambda@Edge for routing based on cookies or headers.
 47|
 48|## Feature Flags
 49|
 50|**How it works**: Deploy code with features wrapped in conditional flags. Toggle features on/off without redeployment.
 51|
 52|**AWS Implementation**:
 53|- **AppConfig**: Feature flags with validation, gradual rollout, and automatic rollback.
 54|- **CloudWatch Evidently**: Feature flags with built-in A/B testing and metric tracking.
 55|
 56|**Best Practices**:
 57|- Use feature flags for incomplete features merged to main (trunk-based development enabler).
 58|- Clean up flags after full rollout; stale flags become technical debt.
 59|- Categorize flags: release flags (temporary), ops flags (kill switches), experiment flags (A/B tests).
 60|- Never put secrets or sensitive config in feature flags.
 61|
 62|## Rollback Strategies
 63|
 64|### Automated Rollback
 65|- Configure CloudWatch alarms on error rate, latency p99, and 5xx count.
 66|- CodeDeploy automatically rolls back when alarms trigger during deployment.
 67|- Lambda: Revert alias to the previous version instantly.
 68|- ECS: CodeDeploy reroutes traffic back to the original target group.
 69|
 70|### Manual Rollback
 71|- Keep the previous artifact (Docker image, Lambda ZIP) tagged and deployable.
 72|- Document the rollback procedure as a runbook: which commands, in what order, who approves.
 73|- Practice rollbacks regularly; an untested rollback is not a rollback plan.
 74|
 75|## Database Migration During Deployment
 76|
 77|The hardest part of zero-downtime deployment is schema changes. Follow the **expand-contract** pattern:
 78|
 79|1. **Expand**: Add new columns/tables/indexes. Do not remove or rename existing ones. Deploy application code that writes to both old and new schemas.
 80|2. **Migrate**: Backfill data from old schema to new schema.
 81|3. **Contract**: After all application versions use the new schema, remove old columns/tables in a later release.
 82|
 83|Never run destructive schema changes (DROP COLUMN, rename) in the same deployment as the application change.
 84|
 85|## Zero-Downtime Deployment Checklist
 86|
 87|- [ ] Load balancer health checks configured with appropriate thresholds
 88|- [ ] Connection draining enabled (deregistration delay: 30-120 seconds)
 89|- [ ] Graceful shutdown handling in application (finish in-flight requests, close DB connections)
 90|- [ ] Database schema changes are backward-compatible
 91|- [ ] Rollback plan tested and documented
 92|- [ ] Monitoring and alarms in place before deployment starts
 93|- [ ] Pre-deployment smoke tests pass in staging
 94|
 95|## Deployment Windows and Freeze Periods
 96|
 97|- Define standard deployment windows (e.g., Tuesday-Thursday 10:00-16:00 local time) when the team is available to monitor.
 98|- Enforce code freeze periods during high-traffic events (Black Friday, product launches) or compliance windows (end of fiscal quarter).
 99|- Emergency hotfixes bypass freeze periods but require incident commander approval and post-deployment review.
100|- Automate freeze enforcement in the pipeline (reject deployments outside approved windows unless override flag is set).
</file-view>

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Way of Working

We use **trunk-based development**. All work merges to `main` via
short-lived feature branches (typically resolved within 1-2 days).
Long-lived branches accumulate merge debt; we avoid them.

For Construction worktrees, the worktree base branch is `main` and the
merge target is `main`.

If our project requires multiple environments (staging, production), we
still keep one trunk and gate releases via tags or environment-specific
deployment configs — not via long-lived release branches.

We **squash-merge** Bolt branches into `main`. Each Bolt becomes one
commit on the trunk, named by the Bolt slug, with the full Bolt commit
history preserved on the source branch until the worktree is discarded.

Squash gives us a clean linear `main` history that maps 1:1 to
delivery-planning's Bolt sequence. We accept the trade-off of losing
intermediate commits on `main` because the audit log preserves the full
event sequence anyway.

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Walking Skeleton

When practices are scope-dependent, we run the walking-skeleton Bolt
**first** only when the active scope file declares `skeleton: on`. Bolt 1
is solo, gated, and the user explicitly approves before remaining Bolts
run.

We **skip the skeleton ceremony** when the active scope file declares
`skeleton: off`. The first Bolt runs like any other — there's nothing to
bootstrap.

After Bolt 1 ships (when it runs), the orchestrator fires the **ladder
prompt**: "How should the remaining Bolts run?" Options: continue
autonomously, gate every Bolt. The team picks per project. The choice
persists as `Construction Autonomy Mode` in `aidlc-state.md`.

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Testing Posture

We treat tests as a first-class deliverable in every Bolt. The specific
methodology (TDD, BDD, ATDD, or classic test-after) is affirmed at
practices-discovery and recorded in `team.md` under this heading with explicit
`Methodology` and `Ordering` fields; Code Generation resolves those fields
independently from coverage, tooling, and scope notes.

When no posture has been affirmed, our default per scope is:
- **Methodology**: test-after
- **Ordering**: implement each applicable testable layer, then write and run
  that layer's tests.
- `mvp`, `enterprise`, `feature`, `infra`, `classic` add an 80% line-coverage
  floor and CI execution before merge.
- `bugfix`, `security-patch` add a targeted regression for the specific
  bug/vulnerability and require the existing suite to remain green.
- `express` uses the Minimal strategy: requirement-driven unit tests (one per
  requirement, with a happy-path floor per component); existing tests remain
  green.
- `poc`, `refactor`, `workshop` add no extra new-test floor and require the
  existing suite to remain green.

The active `Test Strategy` still applies in every scope and determines test
volume/types. Scope floors are additive; they never reduce or replace the
selected strategy.

Build and Test verifies defined coverage floors and affirmed quality targets;
they may not be weakened to make a step pass.

Affirm a stricter posture in `team.md` if the team commits to one.

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Change Control

<!-- Mode: strict or relaxed. Strict here holds for every intent in this space and cannot be changed from chat. -->

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Deployment

We **deploy on merge** to staging environments. Production deploys gate
on a separate manual approval — typically tech lead + product owner
sign-off in CodePipeline or a CD platform's environment protection.

Teams that have invested in test coverage and observability sometimes
graduate to continuous deployment to production (every commit
auto-deploys); that's a team decision, not a framework default.

"},{"path":"aidlc/spaces/default/memory/org.md","text":"## Code Style

We defer to project-level configurations:
- Formatter: Prettier (JS/TS), Black (Python), `gofmt` (Go), or
  language-default. Configured in repo root (`.prettierrc`,
  `pyproject.toml`, etc.).
- Linter: ESLint, Ruff, golangci-lint, etc. Run in CI before merge;
  failure blocks the PR.
- Naming conventions: language idiomatic (camelCase for JS/TS,
  snake_case for Python, etc.). No project-wide rename rules unless
  team affirms one.

When the framework makes a code-style suggestion, agents read the
project's linter config first; the agent's suggestion only fires if the
linter doesn't already cover it.

An unpersisted switch therefore does not outlive its session, which is exactly what persistence buys — a human who wants a switch to survive a resume accepts the ritual, and a human who declines is served correctly for the rest of the session and re-resolved from disk in the next one. A persisted rule NEVER outranks the brief, and never outranks a later explicit human request to switch: it is the fallback for a brief that states no language, and because the learnings write path appends rather than replaces, a superseded language rule can outlive the switch — the LAST conversation-language rule under `## Corrections` is the current one.

This includes the descriptive text of a rule shaped as `ALWAYS …` / `NEVER …`, where the leading marker is a fixed token but the sentence it introduces is not. A Markdown artifact is not English merely because a tool parses part of it: localize the prose that surrounds a preserved token. Verbatim human input echoed into an artifact is always kept exactly as the human wrote it.
- **Conversation language — preserved tokens**: Any literal a stage file or the stage protocol spells in backticks and tells you to write exactly is a fixed token — keep it English, character for character, and localize only the prose around it. This covers option labels and sentinel VALUES, not just syntax: `[Answer]:` tags with their option letters, the mandatory final option `X. Other (please specify)`, the assumption-confirmation options `A. Accept assumptions` / `B. Convert to follow-up questions` (the engine compares the filled answer against the literal), the `None.` / `None` sentinels under `## Assumptions & Open Questions` and `## Positions`, the `AGREE:` / `OBJECT:` position prefixes, and the `**Collaborator:** <agent-slug>` first line the engine matches exactly before it accepts a stage. Glossing such a literal when you PRESENT it to the human is fine; what you WRITE into an artifact is the literal itself. Also preserved: the source-register tags `[desc]`, `[scope]`, `[assumption]`, `[Q<n>]`, `[memory:M<n>]` with their literal prefixes (`Initial description:`, `Workflow-selected scope:`); the H2 headings the claim-sources sensor matches verbatim (`## Sources`, `## Assumptions & Open Questions`, `## Assumption Confirmation`, `## Review`) plus any other H2 taken from a stage template, which the `required-sections` sensor matches verbatim whenever a template is supplied (the framework ships none, so a team's `aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/templates/` is what arms that check); the reviewer verdicts `READY` and `NOT-READY`; YAML keys and enum values inside fenced blocks (`units`, `name`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `service | spec | ui | packaging | library`); the field labels, status values, and checkbox states of `aidlc-state.md` and the audit shards; the verbatim initial description decoded from `<record>/project-description.json` (the `**Project**` state field is only its safe single-line preview); stable IDs (`FR-1`, `ENT-001`, `BR1.1`); enum and classification values; code and identifiers; file paths; mermaid keywords; and cross-references.
