 18|# Developer Agent
 19|
 20|You are a senior software developer specializing in code implementation, build systems, codebase analysis, and data modelling. You translate architectural designs and unit specifications into production-quality code. During reverse engineering, you perform deep code scans to produce structured analysis that the architect synthesizes. You design API contracts, data models, and IaC code. You have Bash access for running build tools, package managers, and test commands.
 21|
 22|## Core Responsibilities
 23|
 24|### Code Generation & Implementation
 25|- Implement units of work according to architectural specifications
 26|- Follow established project conventions (naming, structure, formatting)
 27|- Write idiomatic code for the target language and framework
 28|- Include inline documentation for non-obvious logic
 29|- Produce IaC code (CDK constructs, CloudFormation templates)
 30|
 31|### Reverse Engineering
 32|- Scan project structure to identify languages, frameworks, and build systems
 33|- Classify source files by purpose (model, controller, service, utility, config, test)
 34|- Extract dependency graphs from import/require/include statements
 35|- Identify API endpoints, database models, and external integrations
 36|- Detect code patterns, anti-patterns, and technical debt indicators
 37|
 38|### API & Data Design
 39|- Design API contracts (REST, GraphQL, gRPC) from specifications
 40|- Design data models (relational and NoSQL)
 41|- Execute database migrations and validate data integrity
 42|- Handle serialization, validation, and error mapping at API boundaries
 43|
 44|### Build System & Quality
 45|- Identify package managers and build tools
 46|- Parse dependency manifests for version conflicts and security advisories
 47|- Apply language-specific best practices and idioms
 48|- Ensure consistent error handling patterns
 49|
 50|## Collaboration
 51|
 52|- **Receives from**: architect-agent (unit specifications, design patterns, API specs), quality-agent (test requirements, bug reports)
 53|- **Works with**: architect-agent (clarify design intent), aws-platform-agent (CDK/infrastructure alignment), devsecops-agent (secure coding review)
 54|- **Hands off to**: quality-agent (implemented code for testing), architect-agent (code scan results for RE synthesis)
 55|
 56|*Note: The SKILL.md orchestrator handles all inter-agent delegation. This agent does not invoke other agents directly.*
 57|
 58|## Memory Focus
 59|
 60|`aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/{org,team,project}.md` — active-space guardrails and affirmed practices (read per `.devin/knowledge/aidlc-shared/rules-reading.md`). Consult `## Code Style` for type-hint, formatter, linter, and team-specific conventions. During Code Generation, the fingerprinted `## Testing Contract` embedded in the approved plan is authoritative for methodology and ordering; do not independently re-resolve `## Testing Posture` or replace the approved TDD, BDD, ATDD, test-after, or custom/mixed profile with an inferred convention. If the contract is absent or conflicts with the dispatch marker, stop without generating code.
 61|
 62|## Key Principles
 63|
 64|1. **Working code over perfect code** — Deliver functional, tested implementations. Perform Refactor during initial generation when the approved Testing Contract includes that step (TDD, BDD, ATDD, or custom); otherwise defer opportunistic refactors to subsequent iterations.
 65|2. **Convention over configuration** — Follow the project's existing patterns. Consistency with the codebase trumps personal preference.
 66|3. **Explicit over clever** — Write code that is easy to read and debug. Avoid abstractions that obscure intent.
 67|4. **Fail fast, fail loud** — Validate inputs early. Throw meaningful errors. Never swallow exceptions silently.
 68|5. **Test what matters** — Every generated unit includes at least a happy-path test. Edge cases are covered when the specification calls for them.
 69|6. **Scan before you build** — In reverse engineering, thoroughness of the code scan determines the quality of the architectural synthesis.
</file-view>

  1|# REST API Design Guide
  2|
  3|Practical principles for designing consistent, predictable, and evolvable HTTP APIs.
  4|
  5|## URL Naming Conventions
  6|
  7|- Use plural nouns for collections: `/orders`, `/users`, `/products`
  8|- Nest resources to express ownership: `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}`
  9|- Keep URLs shallow (max 2-3 levels); flatten when relationships are weak
 10|- Use kebab-case for multi-word segments: `/order-items`, not `/orderItems`
 11|- Avoid verbs in URLs; let HTTP methods convey the action
 12|- Use query parameters for filtering, sorting, and pagination: `/orders?status=pending&sort=-createdAt`
 13|
 14|## HTTP Method Semantics
 15|
 16|| Method | Purpose | Idempotent | Safe |
 17||--------|---------|------------|------|
 18|| GET | Retrieve resource(s) | Yes | Yes |
 19|| POST | Create a resource or trigger a process | No | No |
 20|| PUT | Full replace of a resource | Yes | No |
 21|| PATCH | Partial update of a resource | No* | No |
 22|| DELETE | Remove a resource | Yes | No |
 23|
 24|Use POST for actions that do not map to CRUD: `POST /orders/{id}/cancel`.
 25|
 26|## Status Code Usage
 27|
 28|- **200 OK** — Successful GET, PUT, PATCH, or action POST
 29|- **201 Created** — Successful POST that created a resource; include Location header
 30|- **204 No Content** — Successful DELETE or PUT with no response body
 31|- **400 Bad Request** — Malformed syntax or invalid field values
 32|- **401 Unauthorized** — Missing or invalid authentication credentials
 33|- **403 Forbidden** — Authenticated but insufficient permissions
 34|- **404 Not Found** — Resource does not exist
 35|- **409 Conflict** — State conflict (duplicate, version mismatch)
 36|- **422 Unprocessable Entity** — Valid syntax but business rule violation
 37|- **429 Too Many Requests** — Rate limit exceeded; include Retry-After header
 38|- **500 Internal Server Error** — Unhandled server failure
 39|
 40|## Error Response Format
 41|
 42|Use a consistent envelope for every error. Include a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and optional field-level detail:
 43|
 44|```json
 45|{
 46|  "error": {
 47|    "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
 48|    "message": "One or more fields failed validation.",
 49|    "details": [
 50|      { "field": "email", "reason": "Must be a valid email address." }
 51|    ],
 52|    "requestId": "abc-123"
 53|  }
 54|}
 55|```
 56|
 57|Always include a request ID for traceability.
 58|
 59|## Pagination Patterns
 60|
 61|- **Offset-based**: `?offset=20&limit=10` — Simple but degrades on large datasets due to OFFSET cost.
 62|- **Cursor-based**: `?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&limit=10` — Encode the last-seen key as an opaque token. Preferred for DynamoDB and large datasets.
 63|- Return pagination metadata in the response body: `nextCursor`, `hasMore`, `totalCount` (if cheap to compute).
 64|
 65|## Versioning Strategies
 66|
 67|- **URL path versioning** (`/v1/orders`) — Most explicit, easiest for consumers. Preferred for public APIs.
 68|- **Header versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json`) — Cleaner URLs but harder to discover.
 69|- Avoid query-parameter versioning (`?version=2`); it conflates filtering with contract selection.
 70|- Version only when you introduce breaking changes. Additive changes (new optional fields) do not require a new version.
 71|
 72|## OpenAPI and AsyncAPI
 73|
 74|- Maintain an OpenAPI 3.1 spec as the source of truth. Generate server stubs and client SDKs from it.
 75|- For event-driven APIs (SNS, EventBridge, SQS), use AsyncAPI to document message schemas and channel bindings.
 76|- Store specs in the repo alongside the code (`docs/openapi.yaml`) and validate them in CI with spectral or redocly-cli.
 77|
 78|## HATEOAS Considerations
 79|
 80|- Include `_links` in responses to guide clients to related actions and resources.
 81|- Useful for complex state machines (order lifecycle) where available transitions change.
 82|- For internal microservice APIs, HATEOAS is often unnecessary overhead; reserve it for public or partner APIs where discoverability matters.
</file-view>

  1|# Code Analysis Guide
  2|
  3|## Package & Build System Discovery
  4|
  5|Scan the project root and common subdirectories for these markers:
  6|
  7|| File | Build System | Language/Runtime |
  8||------|-------------|-----------------|
  9|| `package.json` | npm/yarn/pnpm | JavaScript/TypeScript |
 10|| `tsconfig.json` | TypeScript compiler | TypeScript |
 11|| `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` / `setup.py` | pip/poetry/setuptools | Python |
 12|| `Cargo.toml` | Cargo | Rust |
 13|| `go.mod` | Go modules | Go |
 14|| `pom.xml` | Maven | Java/Kotlin |
 15|| `build.gradle` / `build.gradle.kts` | Gradle | Java/Kotlin |
 16|| `Gemfile` | Bundler | Ruby |
 17|| `*.csproj` / `*.sln` | dotnet/MSBuild | C# |
 18|| `Makefile` | Make | Any |
 19|| `Dockerfile` / `docker-compose.yml` | Docker | Containerized |
 20|| `serverless.yml` / `template.yaml` | Serverless/SAM | Cloud functions |
 21|| `cdk.json` / `cdktf.json` | CDK/CDKTF | Infrastructure |
 22|
 23|## Framework Detection Patterns
 24|
 25|Identify frameworks by scanning imports and configuration:
 26|- **React**: `import React`, `jsx`/`tsx` files, `react-dom`
 27|- **Next.js**: `next.config.js`, `pages/` or `app/` directory structure
 28|- **Express**: `require('express')`, `app.get/post/use` patterns
 29|- **FastAPI**: `from fastapi import`, `@app.get` decorators
 30|- **Django**: `settings.py` with `INSTALLED_APPS`, `urls.py`, `models.py`
 31|- **Spring Boot**: `@SpringBootApplication`, `application.properties/yml`
 32|- **Rails**: `config/routes.rb`, `app/controllers/`, `ActiveRecord`
 33|
 34|## Source File Classification
 35|
 36|Classify every source file into one of these categories:
 37|- **Model/Entity**: Data structures, database models, DTOs, schemas
 38|- **Controller/Handler**: Request routing, input parsing, response formatting
 39|- **Service/UseCase**: Business logic, orchestration, domain operations
 40|- **Repository/DAO**: Data access, queries, persistence abstraction
 41|- **Utility/Helper**: Cross-cutting functions, formatters, validators
 42|- **Configuration**: App config, environment setup, dependency injection
 43|- **Middleware**: Request/response pipeline (auth, logging, error handling)
 44|- **Test**: Unit tests, integration tests, fixtures, factories
 45|- **Migration**: Database schema changes, data migrations
 46|- **Static/Asset**: Templates, stylesheets, images, static content
 47|
 48|## Dependency Graph Extraction
 49|
 50|For each source file, extract:
 51|1. **Direct imports** -- modules/packages this file depends on
 52|2. **Exported symbols** -- functions/classes/constants this file provides
 53|3. **External dependencies** -- third-party packages used
 54|4. **Circular references** -- files that import each other (flag these)
 55|
 56|Build a dependency adjacency list: `file -> [dependency1, dependency2, ...]`
 57|
 58|## Code Quality Quick Assessment
 59|
 60|Rate each of these on a 3-point scale (good/fair/poor):
 61|- **Naming clarity**: Are variables, functions, and files self-documenting?
 62|- **Function size**: Are functions under 30 lines with single responsibility?
 63|- **Error handling**: Are errors caught, logged, and propagated appropriately?
 64|- **Test presence**: Do critical paths have corresponding test files?
 65|- **Duplication**: Are there copy-paste patterns that should be abstracted?
 66|- **Dead code**: Are there unused imports, unreachable branches, commented-out blocks?

 71|- HTTP method and path (or GraphQL operation name)

 82|- Suppressed linter warnings (`// eslint-disable`, `# noqa`, `@SuppressWarnings`)
 83|- Hard-coded credentials, URLs, or magic numbers

  1|# Code Generation Guide
  2|
  3|## Implementation Pattern Selection
  4|
  5|Choose patterns based on the problem domain:
  6|
  7|| Pattern | When to Use | Avoid When |
  8||---------|-------------|------------|
  9|| **Repository** | Abstracting data access, multiple storage backends | Single database, simple CRUD only |
 10|| **Service Layer** | Coordinating business logic across multiple repositories | Logic fits in a single model method |
 11|| **Factory** | Complex object creation, conditional construction logic | Simple constructor suffices |
 12|| **Strategy** | Runtime behavior variation (e.g., payment processing, notifications) | Only one algorithm exists |
 13|| **Observer/Event** | Decoupling side effects from core logic (email, logging, cache invalidation) | Synchronous response required from all handlers |
 14|| **Middleware/Pipeline** | Cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, validation, rate limiting) | Single-purpose request handling |
 15|| **Adapter** | Wrapping external APIs/SDKs behind a stable internal interface | Internal-only code with no external dependencies |
 16|
 17|## Framework-Specific Generation Strategies
 18|
 19|### General Principles (All Frameworks)
 20|1. Scan existing code for conventions before generating new code
 21|2. Match the project's import style (named vs. default, absolute vs. relative)
 22|3. Follow the project's directory structure conventions
 23|4. Use the project's established error handling pattern
 24|5. Match existing naming conventions (camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase)
 25|
 26|### Web API Implementation Checklist
 27|For each endpoint, generate:
 28|- [ ] Route definition with HTTP method and path
 29|- [ ] Request validation (path params, query params, body schema)
 30|- [ ] Authentication/authorization middleware
 31|- [ ] Service call with error handling
 32|- [ ] Response serialization with correct status code
 33|- [ ] Error response formatting (consistent error envelope)
 34|
 35|### Database Model Checklist
 36|For each entity, generate:
 37|- [ ] Model/schema definition with field types and constraints
 38|- [ ] Indexes for queried fields and foreign keys
 39|- [ ] Timestamps (created_at, updated_at) where appropriate
 40|- [ ] Soft delete support if specified in requirements
 41|- [ ] Migration file for schema changes
 42|- [ ] Seed data for development/testing if applicable
 43|
 44|## Brownfield Modification Best Practices
 45|
 46|When modifying existing codebases (most common scenario):
 47|
 48|### Before Writing Code
 49|1. **Map the change surface**: Identify all files that will be touched
 50|2. **Trace the call chain**: Follow the execution path from entry point to persistence
 51|3. **Check for tests**: Find existing tests that cover the area being modified
 52|4. **Identify conventions**: Note patterns used in surrounding code
 53|
 54|### Modification Rules
 55|- Match the surrounding code's style exactly, even if you prefer another style
 56|- Do not refactor unrelated code in the same change
 57|- Preserve existing function signatures when adding optional parameters
 58|- Add backward-compatible defaults for new configuration
 59|- Update existing tests to cover the changed behavior
 60|- Add new tests for new behavior
 61|
 62|### Common Pitfalls
 63|- Breaking existing imports by renaming or moving files
 64|- Changing a function's return type without updating all callers
 65|- Adding required parameters to public APIs
 66|- Modifying shared utility functions without checking all consumers
 67|- Forgetting to update database migrations for schema changes
 68|
 69|## Testing Patterns
 70|
 71|### Unit Test Structure
 72|Follow the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern:
 73|```
 74|// Arrange: Set up preconditions and inputs
 75|// Act: Execute the unit under test
 76|// Assert: Verify the expected outcome
 77|```
 78|
 79|### What to Test per Unit
 80|
 81|| Unit Type | Test Focus |
 82||-----------|------------|
 83|| Service/Use Case | Business logic correctness, edge cases, error handling |
 84|| Controller/Handler | Request parsing, response format, status codes, auth checks |
 85|| Repository/DAO | Query correctness (use in-memory DB or test containers) |
 86|| Utility/Helper | Input/output mapping, boundary values, null/undefined handling |
 87|| Middleware | Pass-through behavior, rejection conditions, header manipulation |
 88|
 89|### Test Data Strategy
 90|- Use factories/builders for complex objects (avoid raw JSON literals)
 91|- Isolate test data per test (no shared mutable fixtures)
 92|- Use meaningful test data that reflects real scenarios
 93|- Name test variables to express their purpose (`expiredToken`, `adminUser`, `emptyCart`)
 94|
 95|## Code Quality Standards
 96|
 97|### Function Design
 98|- Maximum 30 lines per function (excluding tests)
 99|- Single responsibility: one function does one thing
100|- Maximum 3 parameters; use an options object for more
101|- Return early to avoid deep nesting (guard clauses)
102|- Pure functions where possible (no side effects)
103|
104|### Error Handling
105|- Fail fast: validate inputs at function entry
106|- Use typed/custom errors for domain-specific failures
107|- Never swallow exceptions silently (at minimum, log them)
108|- Propagate errors with context (wrap, do not replace)
109|- Distinguish between recoverable errors (retry) and fatal errors (abort)
110|
111|### Naming Conventions
112|- Functions: verb + noun (`createUser`, `validateInput`, `calculateTotal`)
113|- Booleans: `is`/`has`/`should` prefix (`isActive`, `hasPermission`)
114|- Collections: plural nouns (`users`, `orderItems`)
115|- Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for true constants
116|- Avoid abbreviations unless universally understood (`id`, `url`, `api`)
117|
118|### File Organization
119|- One primary export per file (class, function, or component)
120|- Group related files by feature/domain, not by technical layer
121|- Keep test files adjacent to source files (or in a mirrored `__tests__` directory)
122|- Index files only for public API re-exports, never for internal organization
123|
124|## Automation-Friendly Code Rules
125|
126|### data-testid Attributes
127|Add `data-testid` attributes to all interactive elements to support automated testing (E2E, integration, accessibility audits):
128|
129|- **Required on**: buttons, inputs, links, form elements, modals, dropdowns, tabs, and other interactive containers
130|- **Naming convention**: `{component}-{element-role}` (e.g., `login-form-submit-button`, `user-profile-edit-link`, `settings-modal-close`)
131|- **Rules**:
132|  - Use lowercase kebab-case
133|  - Keep `data-testid` values stable across code changes — do not tie them to dynamic state or auto-generated IDs
134|  - Avoid dynamic or auto-generated IDs (e.g., `button-${index}`) — use semantic names instead
135|  - Group related elements under a container `data-testid` (e.g., `user-table` wrapping `user-table-row-{id}`)
136|  - Apply to both visible and programmatically interactive elements (e.g., hidden file inputs triggered by a button)
</file-view>

  1|# Code Generation Patterns
  2|
  3|## Purpose
  4|Standards and patterns for generating clean, maintainable code. These principles apply regardless of language and ensure generated code is production-worthy, not prototype-quality.
  5|
  6|## Clean Code Principles
  7|
  8|### Naming
  9|- **Variables**: Describe what it holds, not the type. Use `customerEmail` not `str1` or `data`.
 10|- **Functions**: Describe what it does using a verb. Use `calculateShippingCost()` not `process()` or `doWork()`.
 11|- **Booleans**: Use `is`, `has`, `can`, `should` prefixes. Use `isActive` not `active` or `flag`.
 12|- **Constants**: Use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for true constants. Use `MAX_RETRY_COUNT` not `num`.
 13|- **Classes**: Use nouns. Use `OrderProcessor` not `ProcessOrders` or `OrderHelper`.
 14|
 15|### Functions
 16|- Do one thing. If the function name includes "and", split it into two functions.
 17|- Keep parameter count low (0-3 ideal; more than 3 suggests a parameter object is needed).
 18|- Avoid boolean parameters that switch behavior — use two clearly named functions instead.
 19|- Return early for guard clauses to reduce nesting depth.
 20|
 21|### Files
 22|- One primary concept per file (one class, one module, one component).
 23|- Keep files under 300 lines. If longer, the concept is likely doing too much.
 24|- Group related files by feature, not by type (see "Code Organization" below).
 25|
 26|## SOLID Principles Applied
 27|
 28|### Single Responsibility (S)
 29|Each module/class has one reason to change.
 30|```
 31|// Bad: UserService handles auth, profile, and notifications
 32|// Good: AuthService, ProfileService, NotificationService
 33|```
 34|
 35|### Open/Closed (O)
 36|Extend behavior without modifying existing code. Use interfaces and composition.
 37|```
 38|// Bad: Adding a new payment type requires modifying PaymentProcessor
 39|// Good: PaymentProcessor accepts a PaymentStrategy interface; add new strategies without touching the processor
 40|```
 41|
 42|### Liskov Substitution (L)
 43|Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking behavior. If overriding a method changes the contract, the inheritance hierarchy is wrong.
 44|
 45|### Interface Segregation (I)
 46|No client should depend on methods it does not use. Prefer small, focused interfaces over large ones.
 47|```
 48|// Bad: interface Repository { find, save, delete, export, import, backup }
 49|// Good: interface Readable { find }, interface Writable { save, delete }
 50|```
 51|
 52|### Dependency Inversion (D)
 53|High-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. Pass dependencies in; do not construct them internally.
 54|```
 55|// Bad: class OrderService { db = new PostgresDB() }
 56|// Good: class OrderService { constructor(db: Database) }
 57|```
 58|
 59|## Error Handling Patterns
 60|
 61|### Result Type (Preferred)
 62|Return success/failure explicitly instead of throwing exceptions for expected failures.
 63|```typescript
 64|type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
 65|
 66|function parseEmail(input: string): Result<Email, ValidationError> {
 67|  if (!isValidEmail(input)) {
 68|    return { ok: false, error: new ValidationError('Invalid email format') };
 69|  }
 70|  return { ok: true, value: new Email(input) };
 71|}
 72|```
 73|
 74|### Try-Catch Hierarchy
 75|When using exceptions, follow this hierarchy:
 76|1. **Catch specific exceptions first** — handle known, recoverable errors
 77|2. **Let unknown exceptions propagate** — do not catch `Exception` or `Error` broadly
 78|3. **Catch at boundaries** — API handlers, event processors, and CLI entry points are appropriate catch-all locations
 79|4. **Never swallow exceptions silently** — `catch (e) {}` hides bugs
 80|
 81|### Error Messages
 82|- Include what happened, why it happened, and what the user/developer can do about it
 83|- Include relevant context (IDs, input values, operation being performed)
 84|- Do not expose internal implementation details in user-facing errors
 85|
 86|## Logging Standards
 87|
 88|### Log Levels
 89|- **ERROR**: Something failed that requires attention. Include enough context to diagnose.
 90|- **WARN**: Something unexpected happened but was handled. May indicate a developing issue.
 91|- **INFO**: Significant business events (order placed, user registered, payment processed). One per operation.
 92|- **DEBUG**: Detailed diagnostic information for development. Never log sensitive data at any level.
 93|
 94|### Structured Logging
 95|```json
 96|{
 97|  "level": "INFO",
 98|  "message": "Order placed successfully",
 99|  "orderId": "ord-123",
100|  "customerId": "cust-456",
101|  "totalAmount": 99.99,
102|  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
103|  "correlationId": "req-789"
104|}
105|```
106|
107|### Rules
108|- Log at operation boundaries (start, success, failure) — not inside loops
109|- Include correlation/request IDs for tracing across services
110|- Never log: passwords, tokens, API keys, PII, credit card numbers
111|- Use structured format (JSON) not free-text strings for production logs
112|
113|## Input Validation at Boundaries
114|
115|### Boundary Definition
116|Validate input at every trust boundary — where data enters your system from an untrusted source:
117|- API request handlers (HTTP, gRPC, GraphQL)
118|- Event/message consumers (SQS, Kafka, EventBridge)
119|- File upload processors
120|- CLI argument parsers
121|- Database query results from external systems
122|
123|### Validation Strategy
124|```
125|External Input → Validate at boundary → Convert to domain type → Domain logic uses typed values
126|```
127|
128|### What to Validate
129|- **Presence**: Required fields exist and are not null/empty
130|- **Type**: Values are the expected type (string, number, date)
131|- **Range**: Numbers within acceptable bounds, strings within length limits
132|- **Format**: Emails, URLs, dates, phone numbers match expected patterns
133|- **Business rules**: Values are valid in context (status transitions, referential integrity)
134|
135|### After Validation
136|Once data passes the boundary and is converted to a domain type, internal code should NOT re-validate. Trust the boundary. This keeps domain logic clean and focused on business rules.
137|
138|## Code Organization
139|
140|### By Feature (Recommended)
141|```
142|/src
143|  /orders
144|    order.ts              # domain model
145|    order-service.ts      # business logic
146|    order-repository.ts   # data access
147|    order-handler.ts      # API handler
148|    order.test.ts         # tests
149|  /customers
150|    customer.ts
151|    customer-service.ts
152|    ...
153|```
154|
155|### By Layer (Avoid for Medium-Large Projects)
156|```
157|/src
158|  /models        # all domain models from all features
159|  /services      # all services from all features
160|  /repositories  # all repositories from all features
161|  /handlers      # all handlers from all features
162|```
163|
164|### Why Feature-Based is Better
165|- Related code is co-located — changes to "orders" touch files in one directory
166|- Easy to understand the scope of a feature by looking at one directory
167|- Supports extraction to microservices later (each feature directory is a candidate)
168|- Layer-based organization scatters related code across the entire project
169|
170|## Code Generation Checklist
171|- [ ] Follows naming conventions (descriptive, consistent, no abbreviations)
172|- [ ] Functions are small and single-purpose
173|- [ ] Error handling is explicit (Result type or catch at boundaries)
174|- [ ] Input validation at all trust boundaries
175|- [ ] Structured logging at operation boundaries
176|- [ ] No hardcoded secrets, URLs, or configuration values
177|- [ ] Dependencies are injected, not constructed internally
178|- [ ] Tests accompany all generated code
179|- [ ] Code is organized by feature, not by layer
</file-view>

  1|# Data Modelling Patterns
  2|
  3|Guidance for designing data models across relational and NoSQL databases, with emphasis on DynamoDB single-table design.
  4|
  5|## Relational vs NoSQL — When to Choose
  6|
  7|| Factor | Relational (RDS/Aurora) | NoSQL (DynamoDB) |
  8||--------|------------------------|------------------|
  9|| Access patterns | Ad-hoc, complex joins | Known, predictable queries |
 10|| Consistency | Strong ACID transactions | Eventual by default, optional strong |
 11|| Scale model | Vertical (read replicas for reads) | Horizontal, automatic partitioning |
 12|| Schema | Fixed, enforced at DB level | Flexible, enforced in application |
 13|| Cost model | Instance-hours | Request-based (on-demand) or provisioned |
 14|
 15|Choose relational when you need complex reporting, ad-hoc queries, or multi-table transactions. Choose DynamoDB when access patterns are well-defined, you need single-digit-ms latency at any scale, or you want zero operational overhead.
 16|
 17|## Normalization Forms (Relational)
 18|
 19|- **1NF**: Eliminate repeating groups; every column holds atomic values.
 20|- **2NF**: Remove partial dependencies; every non-key column depends on the full primary key.
 21|- **3NF**: Remove transitive dependencies; non-key columns depend only on the primary key, not on other non-key columns.
 22|- **BCNF**: Every determinant is a candidate key.
 23|- Normalize to 3NF for transactional systems. Denormalize selectively for read-heavy workloads (materialized views, read replicas).
 24|
 25|## DynamoDB Single-Table Design
 26|
 27|Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one table using overloaded partition and sort keys.
 28|
 29|**Process**:
 30|1. List all entities and their relationships (user, order, order-item, payment).
 31|2. Document every access pattern with the query it must serve.
 32|3. Design PK/SK patterns to satisfy those queries. Use prefixes: `PK=USER#123`, `SK=ORDER#2024-01-15#456`.
 33|4. Use GSIs to support additional access patterns (inverted index, sparse index).
 34|
 35|**Key Design Rules**:
 36|- Partition key should distribute load evenly; avoid hot partitions.
 37|- Sort key enables range queries and hierarchical data (`SK BEGINS_WITH 'ORDER#'`).
 38|- Use composite sort keys for multi-level queries: `SK=STATUS#pending#DATE#2024-01-15`.
 39|- Store item collections (1:N relationships) under the same partition key for transactional writes.
 40|
 41|## Entity-Relationship Modelling
 42|
 43|- Start with a conceptual ER diagram: entities, attributes, relationships (1:1, 1:N, M:N).
 44|- For M:N relationships in DynamoDB, use an adjacency list pattern: the relationship itself is an item with `PK=ENTITY_A#id`, `SK=ENTITY_B#id`.
 45|- For relational databases, use a join table with foreign keys to both sides.
 46|- Document cardinality and optionality; they drive schema decisions.
 47|
 48|## Index Design
 49|
 50|**DynamoDB GSI/LSI**:
 51|- GSI (Global Secondary Index): Different partition key; eventually consistent. Use for alternate query patterns.
 52|- LSI (Local Secondary Index): Same partition key, different sort key; supports strong consistency. Must be defined at table creation.
 53|- Limit GSIs to 5-8; each consumes additional write capacity.
 54|- Use sparse indexes (only items with the indexed attribute appear) for filtered queries.
 55|
 56|**Relational B-tree Indexes**:
 57|- Index columns that appear in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses.
 58|- Use composite indexes for multi-column queries; put the most selective column first.
 59|- Avoid over-indexing; each index slows writes and consumes storage.
 60|- Use EXPLAIN to validate query plans use the intended index.
 61|
 62|## Schema Versioning
 63|
 64|- Add a `schemaVersion` attribute to every item (DynamoDB) or a `schema_version` column (relational).
 65|- Application code handles backward-compatible reads across versions.
 66|- For relational, use migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase) with numbered, idempotent scripts.
 67|- Never drop columns in production without a deprecation period; add new columns as nullable first.
 68|
 69|## Data Migration Strategies
 70|
 71|- **Dual-write**: Write to old and new stores simultaneously during transition. Complex but zero-downtime.
 72|- **ETL batch migration**: Export, transform, load. Use for one-time moves with a maintenance window.
 73|- **Change data capture (CDC)**: Stream changes from source to target (DynamoDB Streams, RDS event notifications). Best for live migrations.
 74|- Always run migration with a dry-run/validation pass before committing. Compare row counts and checksums.
</file-view>

  1|# Reverse Engineering Artifact Templates
  2|
  3|## Output Structure
  4|
  5|All RE artifacts are created under `aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/codekb/<repo>/` — the durable per-repo code knowledge base shared across intents (the space-level directory the `codekb-path --repo <repo>` tool resolves).
  6|
  7|### Required Artifacts
  8|
  9|1. **business-overview.md** — Business domain context, purpose, key functionality
 10|2. **architecture.md** — System architecture, patterns, component relationships, Mermaid diagrams
 11|3. **code-structure.md** — Package/module organization, file classification, code patterns
 12|4. **api-documentation.md** — External and internal API surfaces, endpoints, contracts
 13|5. **component-inventory.md** — Complete component list with responsibilities and dependencies
 14|6. **technology-stack.md** — Languages, frameworks, libraries with versions
 15|7. **dependencies.md** — External dependencies, internal cross-package dependencies
 16|8. **code-quality-assessment.md** — Test coverage, linting, CI/CD, documentation quality, tech debt
 17|9. **reverse-engineering-timestamp.md** - Records when reverse engineering was performed (date, commit hash if available) plus the structured Scope of Analysis block (template below). The scope block is machine-read by `codekb-scope-diff` on the next rerun, so its accuracy decides whether a future intent can reuse the verified coverage or must merge/replace it.
 18|
 19|### Developer Code Scan Template
 20|
 21|```markdown
 22|## Developer Code Scan Results
 23|
 24|### Scan Coverage
 25|- **Analyzed deeply**: [repo-relative dirs/files actually read and understood, one per line]
 26|- **Skimmed only**: [areas noted at directory granularity without deep reading]
 27|
 28|### Packages Found
 29|- [package name] — [type] — [language] — [purpose]
 30|
 31|### Build System
 32|- **Type**: [build system]
 33|- **Config Files**: [list]
 34|- **Build Dependencies**: [package → package relationships]
 35|
 36|### APIs Discovered
 37|- [API type] — [location] — [endpoints/methods count]
 38|
 39|### Frameworks & Libraries
 40|- [name] — [version] — [purpose]
 41|
 42|### Test Coverage
 43|- **Test Directories**: [list]
 44|- **Test Frameworks**: [list]
 45|- **Coverage Config**: [present/absent]
 46|
 47|### Code Quality Indicators
 48|- **Linting**: [tool and config location]
 49|- **CI/CD**: [pipeline files found]
 50|- **Documentation**: [README presence, doc comments quality]
 51|
 52|### Technical Debt Signals
 53|- [signal description and location]
 54|
 55|## Handoff Summary
 56|- **Intent-relevant finding**: [the finding most relevant to the active intent, with file/line evidence]
 57|- **Risks / follow-up**: [facts the architect or next stage must preserve; "None" if absent]
 58|```
 59|
 60|### Architecture Synthesis Template
 61|
 62|```markdown
 63|## Architecture Analysis
 64|
 65|### System Overview
 66|[High-level description of the system]
 67|
 68|### Architectural Style
 69|[Monolithic / Microservices / Serverless / Hybrid — with evidence]
 70|
 71|### Component Relationships
 72|[Mermaid diagram showing component interactions]
 73|
 74|### Data Flow
 75|[How data moves through the system]
 76|
 77|### Key Design Decisions
 78|[Notable architectural choices and their implications]
 79|
 80|### Improvement Opportunities
 81|[Areas where the architecture could be strengthened]
 82|```
 83|
 84|### Scope of Analysis Block (reverse-engineering-timestamp.md)
 85|
 86|End reverse-engineering-timestamp.md with exactly this fenced block, filled
 87|honestly from the Scan Coverage the developer reported - record what the run
 88|ACTUALLY covered deeply, not what the stage aspired to cover:
 89|
 90|````markdown
 91|## Scope of Analysis
 92|
 93|```yaml
 94|scope_version: 1
 95|kind: partial
 96|intent: [active intent slug]
 97|fingerprint: [output of the mint command in stage Step 3 - verbatim; it prints "unknown" when not computable]
 98|analyzed:
 99|  paths:
100|    - [repo-relative dir (trailing slash) or file analyzed deeply, one per line]
101|  components:
102|    - [component names exactly as they appear in component-inventory.md]
103|shallow:
104|  paths:
105|    - [areas only skimmed]
106|```
107|````
108|
109|Rules:
110|- `kind: full` only when the scan genuinely covered the whole repo deeply; `analyzed.paths` MUST include the repo root (`./`). Anything less is `kind: partial`.
111|- `kind: partial` MUST NOT include `./` in `analyzed.paths`.
112|- `analyzed.paths` entries are repo-relative, directories end with `/`, no glob characters.
113|- Component names must match `component-inventory.md` headings verbatim - the rerun guard compares them literally.
114|- A full rescan wholesale replaces all 9 artifacts and builds this block only from the new run.
115|- For a focused scan of an existing store, read all 9 existing artifacts and the prior Scope of Analysis block first. Update or extend prose for the newly analyzed area and preserve prior prose outside it.
116|- With a CURRENT store, merge `analyzed.paths` and `analyzed.components` as the union of the store and this run. A CURRENT `kind: full` store remains full and retains `./`; otherwise the merged block is partial and cannot claim `./`.
117|- With a STALE or UNVERIFIED store, record only this run in `analyzed.paths` and `analyzed.components`, preserve the prior prose, and demote the store's prior analyzed paths into `shallow.paths`.
118|- With an UNKNOWN_SCOPE legacy store, merge the prior prose best-effort but record only this run in the new scope block.
119|- Mint `fingerprint` over the final `analyzed.paths` in the merged or replaced block.
120|- Build all 9 candidate artifacts under the temporary `<record>/.aidlc-engine/codekb-stage-<repo>/` directory. Never write a cumulative merge directly into the shared CodeKB.
121|- The pre-scan `codekb-snapshot` paths bound verified coverage. If the scan discovers a deep path outside that set, take a new snapshot and repeat the scan over the expanded set.
122|- Publish only through `codekb-publish` with the snapshot's store generation and source fingerprint. A store-generation conflict requires re-reading and re-merging the winner's store; a source conflict requires a fresh scan.
</file-view>

 18|# Operations Agent
 19|
 20|You are a senior site reliability engineer and incident manager specializing in observability, incident response, and operational feedback loops. You ensure that deployed systems are observable, resilient, and continuously improving. You own the operational layer from CloudWatch dashboards and alarms through X-Ray tracing, SLO tracking, incident response runbooks, and chaos engineering validation. You close the feedback loop by channeling production insights back into Ideation for the next iteration. You have Bash access for running monitoring setup commands, runbook scripts, and diagnostic tools.
 21|
 22|## Core Responsibilities
 23|
 24|### Observability Setup
 25|- Design and configure CloudWatch dashboards for system health, latency, error rates, and throughput
 26|- Implement CloudWatch alarms with appropriate thresholds, evaluation periods, and notification targets
 27|- Configure AWS X-Ray tracing for distributed request tracing across services
 28|- Define structured logging standards (JSON, correlation IDs, log levels) and configure log aggregation
 29|- Set up custom metrics for business-critical indicators (transactions per second, conversion rate, queue depth)
 30|
 31|### SLO/SLI Tracking & Error Budgets
 32|- Define Service Level Indicators (SLIs) for each critical user journey (availability, latency, correctness)
 33|- Set Service Level Objectives (SLOs) aligned with business requirements and customer expectations
 34|- Implement error budget tracking and burn-rate alerting
 35|- Define error budget policies (feature freeze when budget is exhausted, relaxed when budget is healthy)
 36|- Produce SLO compliance reports for stakeholder review
 37|
 38|### Incident Response & Runbooks
 39|- Author SSM runbooks for common operational scenarios (service restart, cache flush, failover, scaling)
 40|- Define incident severity levels, response times, and escalation paths
 41|- Establish on-call rotation structure and notification channels
 42|- Conduct post-incident reviews and produce blameless postmortems
 43|- Track incident metrics (MTTR, MTTD, incident frequency) and drive improvements
 44|
 45|### Chaos Engineering & Resilience Validation
 46|- Design chaos experiments for critical failure modes (AZ failure, dependency timeout, disk full, memory pressure)
 47|- Execute controlled chaos experiments in non-production and production environments
 48|- Validate that circuit breakers, retries, and fallbacks operate as designed under failure conditions
 49|- Document resilience gaps discovered through chaos experiments and track remediation
 50|- Build confidence in system resilience through progressive chaos experiment complexity
 51|
 52|### Feedback & Optimization
 53|- Analyze production metrics to identify performance regressions, cost anomalies, and reliability trends
 54|- Channel operational insights back to Ideation as input for the next development cycle
 55|- Recommend infrastructure right-sizing based on actual utilization data
 56|- Identify cost optimization opportunities from production usage patterns
 57|- Propose architectural improvements based on observed failure modes and performance bottlenecks
 58|
 59|## Collaboration
 60|
 61|- **Receives from**: AWS Platform Agent (provisioned infrastructure, CloudWatch namespaces), Pipeline-Deploy Agent (deployed services, deployment metadata)
 62|- **Works with**: AWS Platform Agent (infrastructure tuning, scaling policy adjustments), Quality Agent (performance baselines, SLO validation), Developer Agent (application-level logging, error handling improvements)
 63|- **Hands off to**: Product Agent (operational feedback for next Ideation cycle), Architect Agent (architectural improvement recommendations), orchestrator (feedback report for iteration planning)
 64|
 65|## Memory Focus
 66|
 67|`aidlc/spaces/<active-space>/memory/{org,team,project}.md` -- active-space guardrails and affirmed practices (read per `.devin/knowledge/aidlc-shared/rules-reading.md`). Consult `## Deployment` for release cadence and operational expectations when designing observability, alert thresholds, and runbooks.
 68|
 69|## Key Principles
 70|
 71|1. **Observe everything, alert on what matters** -- Collect comprehensive telemetry but only page humans for user-impacting issues. Alert fatigue degrades incident response faster than missing alerts.
 72|2. **SLOs are the contract with users** -- SLOs define the reliability target. Everything else (error budgets, incident priorities, engineering investment) derives from the SLO.
 73|3. **Incidents are learning opportunities** -- Every incident reveals a gap in observability, resilience, or process. Blameless postmortems convert incidents into system improvements.
 74|4. **Chaos builds confidence** -- Untested resilience mechanisms are assumptions. Chaos engineering converts assumptions into verified capabilities.
 75|5. **Feedback closes the loop** -- Production insights that do not flow back to Ideation are wasted learning. The operations agent is the bridge between what was built and what should be built next.
 76|6. **Toil is the enemy of reliability** -- Manual operational work that is repetitive and automatable must be eliminated. Every runbook step that can be automated should be automated.

  1|# Observability Patterns
  2|
  3|Building visibility into system behaviour through metrics, logs, and traces to enable fast diagnosis and proactive detection.
  4|
  5|## The Three Pillars of Observability
  6|
  7|### 1. Metrics
  8|Numeric measurements aggregated over time. Low cardinality, low cost, ideal for alerting and dashboards.
  9|- **Types**: Counters (always increase), Gauges (can go up/down), Histograms (distribution of values).
 10|- **AWS**: CloudWatch Metrics, CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) for custom metrics from Lambda/ECS.
 11|- Emit custom business metrics: orders placed per minute, payment failures per hour, sign-ups per day.
 12|
 13|### 2. Logs
 14|Timestamped records of discrete events. High cardinality, high volume.
 15|- Use structured logging (JSON) with consistent fields: `timestamp`, `level`, `requestId`, `service`, `message`.
 16|- Correlate logs across services using a shared `requestId` or `traceId` propagated through headers.
 17|- **AWS**: CloudWatch Logs, with Log Groups per service and environment.
 18|
 19|### 3. Traces
 20|End-to-end path of a request through multiple services. Shows latency breakdown and dependency relationships.
 21|- **AWS**: X-Ray for distributed tracing. Auto-instruments SDK calls to AWS services.
 22|- Instrument custom segments for business logic, database queries, and external HTTP calls.
 23|- Use trace maps to visualize service dependencies and identify latency bottlenecks.
 24|
 25|## The Four Golden Signals (Google SRE)
 26|
 27|Monitor these four signals for every service:
 28|
 29|1. **Latency**: Time to serve a request. Measure as percentiles (p50, p95, p99). Track separately for successful and failed requests.
 30|2. **Traffic**: Demand on the system. Requests per second for APIs, messages per second for queues, active connections for WebSocket.
 31|3. **Errors**: Rate of failed requests. Include both explicit errors (5xx) and implicit errors (wrong responses, timeouts, retries).
 32|4. **Saturation**: How full the system is. CPU utilization, memory usage, disk I/O, connection pool usage, Lambda concurrent executions vs reserved concurrency.
 33|
 34|## CloudWatch Dashboards and Alarms
 35|
 36|### Dashboard Design
 37|- One dashboard per service with golden signals at the top.
 38|- Include dependency health: downstream service latency, database connections, queue depth.
 39|- Use CloudWatch Metrics Math for derived metrics: error rate = errors / (errors + successes) * 100.
 40|- Standardize dashboard layouts across services for consistency.
 41|
 42|### Alarm Configuration
 43|- Alarm on symptoms, not causes. Alert on "error rate > 1%" not "CPU > 80%".
 44|- Use composite alarms to reduce noise: only alert when multiple conditions are true simultaneously.
 45|- Set appropriate evaluation periods: avoid single-datapoint alarms that fire on transient spikes. Use `3 out of 5 datapoints` for stability.
 46|- Define alarm actions: SNS notification, Lambda remediation, OpsCenter item creation.
 47|- Severity tiers: P1 (page on-call), P2 (Slack alert, fix within hours), P3 (ticket, fix within sprint).
 48|
 49|## X-Ray Distributed Tracing
 50|
 51|- Enable X-Ray tracing on API Gateway, Lambda, ECS, and SQS.
 52|- Use the X-Ray SDK to create custom subsegments for application logic.
 53|- Add annotations (indexed, searchable) for key dimensions: `customerId`, `orderStatus`, `region`.
 54|- Add metadata (not indexed) for debugging detail: request/response bodies, query parameters.
 55|- Use X-Ray groups and filter expressions to find traces matching specific criteria: `service("payment-service") AND responsetime > 3`.
 56|
 57|## CloudWatch Logs Insights Queries
 58|
 59|Useful query patterns for operational troubleshooting:
 60|
 61|```
 62|# Error rate over time
 63|filter @message like /ERROR/
 64|| stats count() as errors by bin(5m)
 65|
 66|# Slowest requests
 67|filter @duration > 1000
 68|| sort @duration desc
 69|| limit 20
 70|
 71|# Request count by status code
 72|parse @message '"statusCode":*,' as statusCode
 73|| stats count() by statusCode
 74|
 75|# Cold start impact (Lambda)
 76|filter @type = "REPORT"
 77|| stats avg(@duration), max(@duration), avg(@initDuration) by bin(10m)
 78|```
 79|
 80|## Anomaly Detection
 81|
 82|- CloudWatch Anomaly Detection uses ML to establish a baseline and alert on deviations.
 83|- Enable on latency and error rate metrics that have stable patterns.
 84|- Set the detection band width based on acceptable variance (2 standard deviations is a common starting point).
 85|- Combine anomaly detection with static thresholds: anomaly detection catches gradual drift, static thresholds catch acute failures.
 86|
 87|## Log Aggregation and Retention
 88|
 89|- Route all logs to CloudWatch Logs with consistent naming: `/aws/lambda/{service}`, `/ecs/{cluster}/{service}`.
 90|- Set retention policies per log group: 30 days for development, 90 days for staging, 1-3 years for production (or per compliance requirements).
 91|- Archive to S3 for long-term retention and cost optimization. Use Glacier for logs older than 90 days.
 92|- Consider CloudWatch cross-account log aggregation for multi-account setups.
 93|
 94|## Synthetic Monitoring
 95|
 96|- CloudWatch Synthetics canaries: run scripted checks on a schedule (every 1-5 minutes).
 97|- Test critical user journeys: login, place order, view dashboard.
 98|- Canaries run from AWS-managed infrastructure; detect issues before real users report them.
 99|- Alert on canary failure with P1 severity; it means the user-facing path is broken.
100|- Use visual monitoring (screenshot comparison) for UI-heavy applications.
</file-view>

  1|# SLO, SLI, and Error Budget Patterns
  2|
  3|Defining and managing service level objectives using Google SRE principles adapted for AWS environments.
  4|
  5|## Key Terminology
  6|
  7|- **SLI (Service Level Indicator)**: A quantitative measure of a specific aspect of service performance. Example: "the proportion of requests served in under 200ms."
  8|- **SLO (Service Level Objective)**: A target value or range for an SLI. Example: "99.9% of requests will be served in under 200ms, measured over a 30-day rolling window."
  9|- **SLA (Service Level Agreement)**: A contractual commitment to a customer, with consequences for breach. SLAs are looser than SLOs to provide a safety margin.
 10|- **Error Budget**: The allowed amount of unreliability. If SLO is 99.9%, the error budget is 0.1% (approximately 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days).
 11|
 12|## SLI Definition
 13|
 14|Choose SLIs that reflect the user's experience, not internal system metrics.
 15|
 16|### Common SLI Types
 17|
 18|| SLI Type | Definition | Measurement |
 19||----------|-----------|-------------|
 20|| **Availability** | Proportion of successful requests | `(successful requests / total requests) * 100` |
 21|| **Latency** | Proportion of requests faster than threshold | `(requests < 200ms / total requests) * 100` |
 22|| **Throughput** | Requests processed per unit time | CloudWatch metric: `RequestCount` per minute |
 23|| **Error Rate** | Proportion of requests returning errors | `(5xx responses / total responses) * 100` |
 24|| **Freshness** | Proportion of data updated within threshold | Time since last successful sync vs target |
 25|| **Correctness** | Proportion of responses with correct output | Validated against ground truth or invariants |
 26|
 27|### SLI Specification Best Practices
 28|- Measure at the point closest to the user (API Gateway, ALB) not at the application.
 29|- Exclude health check traffic and synthetic monitoring from SLI calculations.
 30|- Use CloudWatch Metrics Math or CloudWatch Contributor Insights for SLI computation.
 31|- Define SLIs per critical user journey, not per API endpoint.
 32|
 33|## SLO Target Setting
 34|
 35|### Process
 36|1. Measure current performance for 2-4 weeks to establish a baseline.
 37|2. Set the SLO slightly below the observed baseline (if p99 latency is consistently 150ms, set SLO at 200ms).
 38|3. Validate with stakeholders that the target aligns with user expectations and business requirements.
 39|4. Start conservative; tighten SLOs as reliability improves and tooling matures.
 40|
 41|### Guidelines
 42|- Do not set SLOs at 100%. It is impossible to achieve and eliminates the error budget for deployments and improvements.
 43|- Typical SLO targets: 99.9% for customer-facing services, 99.5% for internal services, 99% for batch processing.
 44|- Use a 30-day rolling window, not calendar month, to avoid reset-day gaming.
 45|- Document the measurement methodology alongside the target.
 46|
 47|## Error Budgets
 48|
 49|The error budget is the inverse of the SLO: `error budget = 1 - SLO target`.
 50|
 51|### Error Budget Policy
 52|Define what happens when the error budget is consumed:
 53|
 54|| Budget Status | Implication | Action |
 55||--------------|-------------|--------|
 56|| > 50% remaining | Healthy | Normal feature development velocity |
 57|| 25-50% remaining | Caution | Increase deployment monitoring, review recent incidents |
 58|| < 25% remaining | At risk | Slow deployments, prioritize reliability work |
 59|| Exhausted (0%) | Frozen | Halt feature releases, all engineering effort on reliability |
 60|
 61|Error budgets create a shared language between product and engineering: "We can afford to ship this risky feature because we have budget, or we cannot because the budget is low."
 62|
 63|## Burn Rate Alerting
 64|
 65|Instead of alerting when the SLO is breached (too late), alert based on the rate at which the error budget is being consumed.
 66|
 67|- **Burn rate**: How fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the window. A burn rate of 1.0 means the budget will be exactly exhausted at the end of the window.
 68|- **Fast burn (SEV1)**: Burn rate > 14x over 1 hour and > 14x over 5 minutes. The budget will be consumed in ~2 hours. Page immediately.
 69|- **Medium burn (SEV2)**: Burn rate > 6x over 6 hours and > 6x over 30 minutes. The budget will be consumed in ~5 days. Alert during business hours.
 70|- **Slow burn (SEV3)**: Burn rate > 3x over 24 hours and > 3x over 6 hours. The budget will be consumed in ~10 days. Create a ticket.
 71|
 72|Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting (Google SRE workbook approach) to balance sensitivity and specificity.
 73|
 74|## SLO-Based Decision Making
 75|
 76|- **Should we deploy?** Check error budget. If healthy, deploy with normal confidence. If low, add extra validation or delay.
 77|- **Should we invest in reliability?** If the SLO is consistently met with budget to spare, invest in features. If the budget is frequently exhausted, invest in reliability.
 78|- **Should we adopt a new dependency?** Evaluate the dependency's SLO. Your service's SLO cannot exceed its least reliable critical dependency.
 79|- **How much testing is enough?** Test until you are confident the deployment will not consume more than a defined fraction of the error budget.
 80|
 81|## Toil Measurement
 82|
 83|Toil is repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service size.
 84|
 85|- Track time spent on toil weekly: manual deployments, alert response, config changes, scaling actions.
 86|- Target: toil should consume no more than 50% of an operations engineer's time (Google SRE standard).
 87|- Prioritize automation of the most time-consuming toil tasks.
 88|- Report toil reduction as a team metric alongside SLO compliance.
 89|
 90|## SLO Dashboards
 91|
 92|Build a dashboard per service showing:
 93|- Current SLO compliance (percentage) vs target, with the measurement window
 94|- Error budget remaining (absolute and percentage)
 95|- Burn rate trend over the last 7 and 30 days
 96|- SLI time series (latency percentiles, error rate, availability)
 97|- Recent incidents that consumed error budget, with links to postmortems
 98|
 99|Use CloudWatch dashboards with Metrics Math, or export to Grafana for richer visualisation.
</file-view>

  1|# Incident Response Guide
  2|
  3|Structured processes for detecting, responding to, and learning from production incidents.
  4|
  5|## Incident Severity Levels
  6|
  7|| Level | Name | Criteria | Response Time | Examples |
  8||-------|------|----------|---------------|---------|
  9|| **SEV1** | Critical | Complete service outage or data loss affecting all users | < 15 minutes | Production down, data breach, payment processing failure |
 10|| **SEV2** | Major | Significant degradation affecting many users, no workaround | < 30 minutes | Partial outage, error rate > 10%, major feature broken |
 11|| **SEV3** | Minor | Limited impact, workaround available | < 2 hours | Non-critical feature broken, intermittent errors, slow performance |
 12|| **SEV4** | Low | Cosmetic or minor issue, no user impact | Next business day | UI glitch, non-critical log errors, minor config drift |
 13|
 14|## Escalation Matrix
 15|
 16|Define who to contact at each severity level:
 17|
 18|| Severity | Primary Responder | Escalation (30 min) | Escalation (1 hour) |
 19||----------|------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
 20|| SEV1 | On-call engineer | Engineering manager + Incident commander | VP Engineering + Stakeholder communication |
 21|| SEV2 | On-call engineer | Team lead | Engineering manager |
 22|| SEV3 | On-call engineer | Team lead (if unresolved in 4 hours) | — |
 23|| SEV4 | Any team member | — | — |
 24|
 25|## On-Call Rotation
 26|
 27|- Rotate weekly among team members. Ensure at least 2 people are trained for on-call at all times.
 28|- Primary and secondary on-call: secondary takes over if primary is unreachable within 10 minutes.
 29|- On-call handoff includes: review of active alerts, ongoing issues, recent deployments, and known risks.
 30|- Compensate on-call fairly: time off in lieu, on-call stipend, or both.
 31|- Maximum on-call frequency: no more than 1 week in 4. If the team is too small, address staffing.
 32|
 33|## Incident Commander Role
 34|
 35|For SEV1 and SEV2 incidents, designate an Incident Commander (IC) who:
 36|- **Coordinates** response efforts; does not debug directly.
 37|- **Communicates** status updates to stakeholders at regular intervals (every 15-30 minutes).
 38|- **Delegates** workstreams: investigation, mitigation, communication, documentation.
 39|- **Decides** when to escalate, when to roll back, when to declare resolution.
 40|- **Documents** timeline, actions taken, and decisions made in a shared incident channel.
 41|
 42|The IC is not necessarily the most senior engineer; it is the person who can coordinate effectively under pressure.
 43|
 44|## Communication During Incidents
 45|
 46|### Internal
 47|- Create a dedicated Slack/Teams channel: `#incident-YYYY-MM-DD-short-description`.
 48|- Post structured updates: **Status** (investigating/identified/mitigating/resolved), **Impact** (who is affected), **Next Step** (what we are doing), **ETA** (when the next update will be).
 49|- Keep the channel focused; move side discussions to threads.
 50|
 51|### External
 52|- SEV1: Status page update within 20 minutes. Customer communication within 1 hour.
 53|- SEV2: Status page update within 1 hour if customer-visible.
 54|- Use pre-drafted templates for common scenarios: "We are experiencing elevated error rates..."
 55|- Never speculate about root cause in external communications until confirmed.
 56|
 57|## Post-Incident Review (Blameless Postmortem)
 58|
 59|Conduct within 48 hours of incident resolution for SEV1/SEV2.
 60|
 61|### Structure
 62|1. **Timeline**: Minute-by-minute account from detection to resolution.
 63|2. **Impact**: Users affected, duration, financial/data impact.
 64|3. **Root Cause**: Technical cause(s) of the incident.
 65|4. **Contributing Factors**: Process, tooling, or knowledge gaps that allowed the incident.
 66|5. **What Went Well**: Effective parts of the response.
 67|6. **What Could Be Improved**: Gaps in detection, response, or communication.
 68|7. **Action Items**: Specific, assigned, time-boxed improvements.
 69|
 70|### Blameless Principles
 71|- Focus on systems and processes, not individuals.
 72|- People made the best decisions they could with the information available.
 73|- Ask "what" and "how", not "who".
 74|- The goal is to improve the system so the same failure cannot recur.
 75|
 76|## SSM Automation Runbooks
 77|
 78|Create automated runbooks for common operational tasks and incident responses:
 79|
 80|- **Restart service**: ECS task restart, Lambda function redeployment.
 81|- **Scale out**: Increase desired count, adjust auto-scaling thresholds.
 82|- **Database failover**: Trigger RDS failover, verify application reconnection.
 83|- **Clear queue backlog**: Increase consumer concurrency, purge DLQ after inspection.
 84|- **Rotate credentials**: Update secrets in Secrets Manager, trigger dependent service reloads.
 85|
 86|Store runbooks as SSM Automation documents in version control. Reference them in alarm actions for automated remediation.
 87|
 88|## Automated Remediation Patterns
 89|
 90|- CloudWatch alarm triggers Lambda function to restart unhealthy ECS tasks.
 91|- Auto Scaling policies respond to custom metrics (queue depth, error rate) not just CPU.
 92|- EventBridge rules detect specific error patterns and invoke Step Functions for multi-step remediation.
 93|- Always include circuit breakers: limit automated remediation attempts (max 3 restarts in 10 minutes) to prevent remediation loops.
 94|
 95|## RTO and RPO Targets
 96|
 97|- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**: Maximum acceptable downtime. How quickly must the system be restored?
 98|- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**: Maximum acceptable data loss. How much data can we afford to lose?
 99|
100|| Tier | RTO | RPO | Strategy |
101||------|-----|-----|----------|
102|| Critical (payments, auth) | < 5 minutes | 0 (zero data loss) | Multi-AZ active-active, synchronous replication |
103|| High (order processing) | < 30 minutes | < 5 minutes | Multi-AZ with automated failover, point-in-time recovery |
104|| Standard (reporting, analytics) | < 4 hours | < 1 hour | Regular backups, automated restoration |
105|| Low (internal tools) | < 24 hours | < 24 hours | Daily backups, manual restoration |
106|
107|Test RTO/RPO targets quarterly through game days and disaster recovery drills.
</file-view>

  1|# NFR Performance and Scalability Guide
  2|
  3|> This guide supplements the full NFR Requirements Guide held by the Security Engineer (lead agent for the NFR Requirements stage). It provides the DevOps Engineer with the performance and scalability sections needed for infrastructure-focused contributions during NFR Requirements and NFR Design stages.
  4|
  5|## Performance Requirement Benchmarking
  6|
  7|### How to Define Performance Requirements
  8|Every performance requirement must specify:
  9|- **Metric**: What is being measured (response time, throughput, resource usage)
 10|- **Target**: The quantitative threshold
 11|- **Percentile**: Which percentile the target applies to (p50, p95, p99)
 12|- **Load condition**: Under what concurrency/traffic the target must hold
 13|- **Measurement method**: How and where the metric is captured
 14|
 15|### Common Performance Targets by Application Type
 16|
 17|| Application Type | Metric | Target | Percentile | Notes |
 18||-----------------|--------|--------|------------|-------|
 19|| Web application (interactive) | Page load time | < 2s | p95 | First contentful paint |
 20|| REST API (synchronous) | Response time | < 200ms | p99 | Excludes network transit |
 21|| Search query | Result delivery | < 500ms | p95 | Including ranking |
 22|| Batch processing | Throughput | N records/min | Average | Define minimum acceptable rate |
 23|| Real-time messaging | End-to-end latency | < 100ms | p99 | From send to delivery |
 24|| File upload | Processing time | < 5s per MB | p95 | Post-upload processing |
 25|
 26|### Performance Anti-Requirements
 27|Explicitly exclude unreasonable expectations:
 28|- "The system should be fast" (not measurable)
 29|- "All pages load instantly" (no target, no percentile)
 30|- "Handle unlimited users" (no capacity boundary)
 31|
 32|Replace with: "The dashboard page loads in < 3 seconds at p95 under 500 concurrent users."
 33|
 34|## Scalability Assessment Frameworks
 35|
 36|### Capacity Planning Template
 37|
 38|| Dimension | Current | 6-Month Target | 12-Month Target | Scaling Mechanism |
 39||-----------|---------|---------------|-----------------|-------------------|
 40|| Concurrent users | N | N * X | N * Y | Horizontal auto-scaling |
 41|| Data volume | N GB | N * X GB | N * Y GB | Partitioning strategy |
 42|| Requests per second | N | N * X | N * Y | Load balancer + replicas |
 43|| Storage growth rate | N GB/month | N * X GB/month | N * Y GB/month | Tiered storage policy |
 44|
 45|### Scalability Requirement Format
 46|```
 47|NFR-SCALE-NNN: [Scalability Requirement]
 48|Current baseline: [measured current capacity]
 49|Target capacity: [required capacity at specific timeline]
 50|Growth model: [linear, exponential, seasonal, step-function]
 51|Scaling approach: [horizontal, vertical, partitioning, caching]
 52|Cost constraint: [infrastructure cost must remain below $X/month at target scale]
 53|Degradation policy: [what degrades first when approaching capacity limits]
 54|```
 55|
 56|### Scaling Decision Matrix
 57|
 58|| Signal | Scale Up | Scale Out | Optimize First |
 59||--------|----------|-----------|----------------|
 60|| CPU consistently > 70% | Single-instance workloads | Stateless services | Check for inefficient algorithms |
 61|| Memory pressure | In-memory processing | Distributed cache | Check for memory leaks |
 62|| I/O wait > 30% | Faster storage tier | Read replicas, sharding | Query optimization, indexing |
 63|| Queue depth growing | Faster consumers | More consumer instances | Batch size tuning |
 64|| Connection pool exhausted | Larger pool size | Connection multiplexing | Connection leak investigation |
</file-view>
